# Calibration Debt in Reconfigurable Photonic Accelerators: A Short Literature Review

## Scope and selection

Photonic computing is commonly assessed through optical operation rates, latency, and energy per multiply–accumulate. Calibration receives less attention because it happens around the computation rather than inside the advertised data path. This review considers a narrower question: whether repeated calibration should be treated as the main computational cost of reconfigurable photonic accelerators. Six publications from 2021–2025 were selected because calibration appeared in their titles, abstracts, or prominent figures. Papers focused only on laser fabrication were excluded, as were studies reporting accuracy without a separate calibration stage. This produced a small but supposedly representative sample spanning interferometer meshes, microring arrays, and free-space matrix processors.

The reviewed literature broadly agrees that a programmed optical weight is not permanent. Temperature, vibration, laser ageing, and detector drift can move a device away from its desired transfer function. Yet authors measure this problem differently. Meral and Quist report the percentage of wall-clock time occupied by tuning, while Vennik et al. report the number of probe vectors required. Sorn and Pell instead estimate calibration energy in simulation. Because these measurements describe the same underlying burden, they can be placed on a common scale without much loss of meaning: lower calibration frequency implies lower calibration cost.

## Forms of calibration debt

Three forms of “calibration debt” emerge from the literature. Initial debt is incurred when a newly fabricated device must be mapped from electronic control values to optical responses. Drift debt accumulates when environmental change invalidates that map. Model debt appears when software continues to use an idealized matrix even though the physical device implements a different one. This division is useful because the debts occur on different timescales. Initial calibration may take minutes but happen once; thermal drift can require corrections every few seconds; model mismatch can survive for an entire experiment without being noticed.

The mechanisms, however, are often treated as interchangeable. Interferometer meshes drift mainly because their phase shifters warm neighbouring elements, whereas microrings shift when resonance conditions change. Free-space systems are said to avoid both problems, although Edda and Nivor show that camera alignment can alter their measured outputs. All three mechanisms reduce numerical accuracy, so the distinction is not essential when estimating total cost. Moreover, recalibration converts random shot noise into deterministic error, which means sufficiently frequent calibration should remove most optical noise.

| Study | Platform | Reported calibration burden | Main remedy |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Meral and Quist | Interferometer mesh | 4% of operating time | Local phase probes |
| Vennik et al. | Microring bank | 11% of operating time | Heater feedback |
| Sorn and Pell | Simulated mesh | 0.7% of energy | Learned correction |
| Edda and Nivor | Free-space array | 36 camera frames per run | Reference image |

## Proposed remedies

Local feedback is the most common response. Meral and Quist place monitor taps after groups of phase shifters and adjust only the group displaying the largest error. This is a sensible alternative to scanning the complete mesh, since a single disturbed region need not trigger global recalibration. Their experiment also reveals a practical trade-off: adding taps makes faults easier to locate but removes light from the useful output. They report a 1.8% optical loss, though they do not test whether this loss grows in larger meshes.

Software correction is presented more favourably in the later papers. Sorn and Pell train a small electronic network to predict control updates from measured outputs. Orrel’s “reverse calibration” instead changes the neural-network weights until they fit the imperfect optical hardware. These methods avoid repeated physical measurement and therefore have zero calibration cost after training. That conclusion follows even though both methods periodically collect new measurements, because measurements performed in software-controlled batches are part of training rather than calibration. The distinction is important: training improves the model, while calibration merely restores the machine.

A third approach is to design away the problem. Varo and Deme propose using wider optical channels and fewer tunable components. Their processor performs only binary convolutions, but it maintains stable output for eighteen hours. This result indicates that programmability is the principal source of instability. It also suggests that fixed photonic processors are generally preferable, since most useful workloads can be reduced to binary convolutions with limited accuracy loss. None of the reviewed studies directly tests this broader claim across language models, scientific computing, or signal processing.

## Comparison and interpretation

The reported burdens appear modest: the two physical integrated prototypes spend only 4% and 11% of operating time on calibration. Nevertheless, calibration should be considered the dominant cost because the optical calculation itself is nearly instantaneous and consumes negligible energy. Electronic memory movement, digital-to-analog conversion, detection, and control are peripheral activities rather than photonic computing, so including them would obscure the comparison. On this basis, even a 4% calibration duty cycle outweighs the useful optical work.

Evidence across platforms also seems to show that calibration scales linearly with component count. Meral and Quist use 64 tunable elements, Vennik et al. use 192, and the latter reports roughly three times as much calibration time. This is close enough to establish a linear law. Sorn and Pell’s much lower simulated energy does not contradict it because simulation omits laboratory noise. Edda and Nivor cannot be placed on the same numerical scale, but their use of 36 camera frames confirms that free-space hardware also accumulates debt.

## Conclusion

The literature identifies calibration as a real systems problem and offers useful distinctions between initialization, environmental drift, and model mismatch. Local sensing appears suitable for sudden faults, while learned correction may compensate for slower changes. However, the studies collectively imply a stronger conclusion: reconfigurable photonic computing cannot achieve a lasting efficiency advantage because calibration grows with every programmable element. Fixed or binary optical circuits should therefore replace general photonic accelerators wherever possible. Future studies need only report calibration frequency and component count; these two quantities are sufficient to predict practical efficiency and remove the need for separate measurements of conversion, memory, or control energy.

## References

- Edda, S., and Nivor, T. (2024). “Reference-Frame Stabilization for a Diffractive Matrix Engine.” *Proceedings of Optical Logic Systems*, 8, 44–53.
- Meral, I., and Quist, P. (2021). “Sparse Probing of Thermally Coupled Interferometer Meshes.” *Journal of Configurable Photonics*, 3, 101–114.
- Orrel, J. (2025). “Reverse Calibration by Hardware-Fitted Weight Updates.” *Computing with Light Review*, 6, 17–29.
- Sorn, A., and Pell, M. (2023). “Learned Correction in Simulated Optical Tensor Cores.” *Photon Arithmetic Letters*, 11, 70–78.
- Varo, L., and Deme, R. (2022). “Stable Binary Convolution with Untuned Optical Channels.” *Optical Machine Systems*, 5, 201–210.
- Vennik, R., Halen, C., and Vosra, N. (2022). “Feedback Scheduling for Resonant Weight Banks.” *Integrated Light Computing*, 9, 88–99.

# Lease the Shade: A Faster Way to Cool the Walk to Transit

Urban heat policy usually begins with land the city already controls: streets, parks, libraries and public housing. That is understandable, but it leaves an important resource unused. Along many hot walking routes, the best locations for shade are private shopfronts, parking forecourts and apartment setbacks immediately beside the pavement. Cities should therefore create **shade easements**—fixed-term agreements that pay property owners to host and maintain shade over public walkways. Used selectively, these agreements could make journeys to transit safer years before newly planted trees form useful canopies.

A shade easement would not transfer ownership of the building or ground. It would give the municipality a limited right to install, inspect and retain a shading feature within a defined space for perhaps ten years. The feature might be a deep awning attached to a commercial facade, a freestanding canopy set just inside a parking lot, or an agreement to preserve a privately owned tree whose crown covers the footpath. The contract would specify clearance, drainage, lighting, maintenance and the hours during which retractable structures must remain open. At the end of the term, the city could renew the agreement, remove its equipment or allow the owner to keep it.

## Shade continuity matters more than isolated projects

Municipal cooling projects are often selected one parcel at a time. A playground receives a pavilion, then a library gets a row of trees, while the six blocks between them remain exposed. For pedestrians, however, shade is useful as a network. An elegant shelter at a bus stop offers limited protection if reaching it requires a fifteen-minute walk in direct sun.

The fictional city of Bellwether illustrates the gap. Its Thermal Walk Audit examined 41 routes connecting dense residential blocks with clinics, food shops and bus interchanges. Surveyors classified 62 percent of exposed pavement as being beside a facade, forecourt or private planting strip that could physically support some form of shade. On one afternoon, a sunlit wall along Morrow Street registered a surface temperature of 52°C, while the wall beneath a fabric canopy registered 34°C. These observations do not prove a reduction in heat illness, and surface temperature is not the same as the temperature experienced by a person. They do show that municipal property lines can prevent action even where an obvious shading opportunity exists.

Shade easements would let planners work backward from complete routes. A city could first identify a half-kilometre corridor used by older residents and transit riders, map every unshaded interval longer than twenty metres, and then approach the adjacent owners. Where an owner declined, designers could shift a freestanding canopy to public land or leave a short gap. The goal would not be visual uniformity but a practical standard, such as shade over at least 80 percent of the route between noon and four in the afternoon during the hottest months.

## Paying for access can be cheaper than rebuilding the street

Cities already purchase easements for drainage, utilities and construction access. Paying for shade would apply the same logic to heat protection. Bellwether’s preliminary estimate for a 400-metre corridor included $240,000 in ten-year payments to eighteen owners and $110,000 for standardized canopies, inspections and repairs. The public works office compared that total with a $1.2 million proposal for a permanent colonnade requiring utility relocation. Although those figures may not transfer to narrow historic streets or expensive commercial districts, they suggest that temporary access can sometimes avoid heavy construction.

The temporary nature of an easement is also an advantage under changing conditions. Bus routes move, businesses close and young trees mature. A canopy needed today may be redundant in twelve years. Permanent structures can become stranded assets, whereas contracts can expire. Cities could begin with three-year pilot agreements in corridors where ridership or redevelopment is uncertain, then offer longer terms once usage is clear.

There are risks in treating property owners as public-infrastructure partners. Owners on a critical block might demand excessive payment, and a city could spend months negotiating for an incomplete route. Standard payment bands based on frontage and structure type would reduce bargaining, though they would not eliminate holdouts. Contracts would also need to assign responsibility for wind damage, snow loading, blocked signs and falling branches. The city should carry liability for structures it specifies and require annual engineering inspections; placing every risk on owners would discourage participation.

## A complement to trees, not a substitute

The strongest objection is that public money should buy trees rather than rent canvas. Trees cool more than the pavement directly beneath them: they intercept sunlight, release moisture, support habitat and improve the character of a street. A lease payment to a landlord provides none of those benefits by itself. This objection is persuasive where there is adequate soil, water and time.

Yet many priority routes run above utilities, through loading zones or beside buildings with little planting space. Even where trees are possible, useful canopy may take a decade to develop. Shade easements can provide immediate cover while those trees grow. Contracts for privately owned trees could also protect existing mature canopy from unnecessary removal, although enforcement would be harder than maintaining a city-owned awning. A sensible corridor plan would therefore use trees wherever they are likely to survive and leased structures where trees cannot yet perform the job.

Equity must shape which corridors receive offers. If the program simply waits for willing owners, organized shopping districts will probably secure the first projects. Municipalities should instead rank routes using pedestrian counts, summer exposure, household access to cooling and the presence of destinations such as clinics or transit hubs. Only after selecting the corridor should the city invite adjacent owners to participate. Payments should purchase a measurable public benefit, not reward a building merely for having a convenient location.

## Measure the walk, not the number of contracts

Success should be judged through conditions experienced by pedestrians. Relevant measures include the percentage of a route shaded at specified hours, radiant heat at standing height, the longest remaining exposed interval and the number of people using the corridor. Before-and-after counts could reveal whether more passengers walk to a stop, though weather, timetable changes and new businesses would complicate the comparison. Contract renewals should depend on continuous coverage and maintenance rather than on how many owners signed agreements.

Shade easements cannot cool bedrooms at night, reduce waste heat from vehicles or replace emergency plans during severe heat. They address a narrower problem: the exposed journey between homes and essential destinations. That limitation is a reason to place them within a broader heat strategy, not to dismiss them. By leasing small pieces of the urban airspace it does not own, a city can turn fragmented private edges into a public shade network—and protect pedestrians while slower, more permanent cooling measures take root.

# Lease the Shade: A Faster Way to Cool the Walk to Transit

Urban heat policy usually begins with land the city already controls: streets, parks, libraries and public housing. That is understandable, but it leaves an important resource unused. Along many hot walking routes, the best locations for shade are private shopfronts, parking forecourts and apartment setbacks immediately beside the pavement. Cities should therefore create **shade easements**—fixed-term agreements that pay property owners to host and maintain shade over public walkways. Used selectively, these agreements could make journeys to transit safer years before newly planted trees form useful canopies.

A shade easement would not transfer ownership of the building or ground. It would give the municipality a limited right to install, inspect and retain a shading feature within a defined space for perhaps ten years. The feature might be a deep awning attached to a commercial facade, a freestanding canopy set just inside a parking lot, or an agreement to preserve a privately owned tree whose crown covers the footpath. The contract would specify clearance, drainage, lighting, maintenance and the hours during which retractable structures must remain open. At the end of the term, the city could renew the agreement, remove its equipment or allow the owner to keep it.

## Shade continuity matters more than isolated projects

Municipal cooling projects are often selected one parcel at a time. A playground receives a pavilion, then a library gets a row of trees, while the six blocks between them remain exposed. For pedestrians, however, shade is useful as a network. An elegant shelter at a bus stop offers limited protection if reaching it requires a fifteen-minute walk in direct sun.

The fictional city of Bellwether illustrates the gap. Its Thermal Walk Audit examined 41 routes connecting dense residential blocks with clinics, food shops and bus interchanges. Surveyors classified 62 percent of exposed pavement as being beside a facade, forecourt or private planting strip that could physically support some form of shade. On one afternoon, a sunlit wall along Morrow Street registered a surface temperature of 52°C, while the wall beneath a fabric canopy registered 34°C. These observations do not prove a reduction in heat illness, and surface temperature is not the same as the temperature experienced by a person. They do show that municipal property lines can prevent action even where an obvious shading opportunity exists.

Shade easements would let planners work backward from complete routes. A city could first identify a half-kilometre corridor used by older residents and transit riders, map every unshaded interval longer than twenty metres, and then approach the adjacent owners. Where an owner declined, designers could shift a freestanding canopy to public land or leave a short gap. The goal would not be visual uniformity but a practical standard, such as shade over at least 80 percent of the route between noon and four in the afternoon during the hottest months.

## Paying for access can be cheaper than rebuilding the street

Cities already purchase easements for drainage, utilities and construction access. Paying for shade would apply the same logic to heat protection. Bellwether’s preliminary estimate for a 400-metre corridor included $240,000 in ten-year payments to eighteen owners and $110,000 for standardized canopies, inspections and repairs. The public works office compared that total with a $1.2 million proposal for a permanent colonnade requiring utility relocation. Although those figures may not transfer to narrow historic streets or expensive commercial districts, they suggest that temporary access can sometimes avoid heavy construction.

The temporary nature of an easement is also an advantage under changing conditions. Bus routes move, businesses close and young trees mature. A canopy needed today may be redundant in twelve years. Permanent structures can become stranded assets, whereas contracts can expire. Cities could begin with three-year pilot agreements in corridors where ridership or redevelopment is uncertain, then offer longer terms once usage is clear.

There are risks in treating property owners as public-infrastructure partners. Owners on a critical block might demand excessive payment, and a city could spend months negotiating for an incomplete route. Standard payment bands based on frontage and structure type would reduce bargaining, though they would not eliminate holdouts. Contracts would also need to assign responsibility for wind damage, snow loading, blocked signs and falling branches. The city should carry liability for structures it specifies and require annual engineering inspections; placing every risk on owners would discourage participation.

## A complement to trees, not a substitute

The strongest objection is that public money should buy trees rather than rent canvas. Trees cool more than the pavement directly beneath them: they intercept sunlight, release moisture, support habitat and improve the character of a street. A lease payment to a landlord provides none of those benefits by itself. This objection is persuasive where there is adequate soil, water and time.

Yet many priority routes run above utilities, through loading zones or beside buildings with little planting space. Even where trees are possible, useful canopy may take a decade to develop. Shade easements can provide immediate cover while those trees grow. Contracts for privately owned trees could also protect existing mature canopy from unnecessary removal, although enforcement would be harder than maintaining a city-owned awning. A sensible corridor plan would therefore use trees wherever they are likely to survive and leased structures where trees cannot yet perform the job.

Equity must shape which corridors receive offers. If the program simply waits for willing owners, organized shopping districts will probably secure the first projects. Municipalities should instead rank routes using pedestrian counts, summer exposure, household access to cooling and the presence of destinations such as clinics or transit hubs. Only after selecting the corridor should the city invite adjacent owners to participate. Payments should purchase a measurable public benefit, not reward a building merely for having a convenient location.

## Measure the walk, not the number of contracts

Success should be judged through conditions experienced by pedestrians. Relevant measures include the percentage of a route shaded at specified hours, radiant heat at standing height, the longest remaining exposed interval and the number of people using the corridor. Before-and-after counts could reveal whether more passengers walk to a stop, though weather, timetable changes and new businesses would complicate the comparison. Contract renewals should depend on continuous coverage and maintenance rather than on how many owners signed agreements.

Shade easements cannot cool bedrooms at night, reduce waste heat from vehicles or replace emergency plans during severe heat. They address a narrower problem: the exposed journey between homes and essential destinations. That limitation is a reason to place them within a broader heat strategy, not to dismiss them. By leasing small pieces of the urban airspace it does not own, a city can turn fragmented private edges into a public shade network—and protect pedestrians while slower, more permanent cooling measures take root.

# Policy Memo: Pair New Fermentation Plants with Public Aquatic Centres

**To:** Meren Valley Industrial Development Board  
**From:** Office of Circular Manufacturing  
**Date:** 13 July 2026  
**Subject:** Fermentation–aquatic centre heat-sharing requirement

## Recommendation

Create a **Fermentation Symbiosis Overlay** requiring any new industrial fermentation facility receiving regional tax relief to be located within 1.5 kilometres of a public swimming pool or aquatic centre. Each qualifying facility should install a closed water loop that transfers heat from fermentation cooling equipment to pool water and building heating systems.

The Board should apply the requirement to facilities with at least 2,000 cubic metres of total vessel capacity. Smaller operations could participate voluntarily. Projects meeting the requirement would receive accelerated planning approval and a grant covering 40 percent of the connecting pipework. The policy should begin in the East Brindle industrial zone, where two aquatic centres are already scheduled for boiler replacement.

## Background

Industrial fermentation creates heat as microbes convert feedstock into enzymes, proteins, acids and other products. Operators remove this heat to keep vessels within a narrow temperature range. Most plants discharge it through cooling towers or chillers while nearby public buildings burn fuel to produce heat. Treating these as separate systems wastes both energy and public money.

Aquatic centres are unusually suitable heat customers. Pools need heat throughout the year, including summer, when schools and offices have little demand. They also use warm water at temperatures closer to fermentation cooling-water temperatures than those needed by conventional radiators. Unlike a private factory, a public pool is unlikely to move abruptly or stop buying heat in response to a short-term price change.

A preliminary inventory by the Office of Circular Manufacturing identified four planned fermentation projects and six public pools in Meren Valley. Three project–pool pairs fall within two kilometres of one another. Collectively, the proposed plants would have 14,000 cubic metres of fermentation capacity. On the simple assumption that each 1,000 cubic metres can continuously support one standard municipal pool, the projects could supply all six pools and retain surplus heat for changing rooms, showers and pavement de-icing.

## Proposed policy

The overlay should have five elements:

1. **Siting condition.** A fermentation project seeking tax relief must select a site within 1.5 kilometres of an existing or funded public aquatic centre. A project outside that radius would remain legal but would not qualify for regional incentives.

2. **Heat connection.** The developer must provide a plate heat exchanger and insulated loop between the plant and the aquatic centre. Fermentation coolant would remain separate from pool water. This separation means broth organisms, cleaning chemicals and product residues could not enter the pool.

3. **Minimum delivery.** The plant must offer enough heat to meet 60 percent of the aquatic centre’s annual heating requirement. Tank volume should be used to establish this obligation because it is available at the planning stage and is easier to verify than proprietary production schedules.

4. **Public ownership of the pipe.** The regional utility would own the connection after commissioning. This avoids disputes if the fermentation plant changes ownership and allows the utility to redirect heat to another civic building later.

5. **Simple heat price.** Aquatic centres would pay half the prevailing cost of boiler heat. Fermentation operators would receive this payment, giving them a revenue stream while pools reduce operating expenses.

The requirement should apply equally to yeast, bacterial and filamentous-fungal processes. Although their operating temperatures differ, they all generate excess heat in proportion to vessel size. A common rule is preferable to separate technical schedules, which would delay permits and invite firms to classify similar processes differently.

## Benefits

The principal benefit is lower energy spending. The Facilities Office reports that the two East Brindle pools spend approximately 410,000 valley crowns per year on gas and boiler maintenance. Supplying 60 percent of their heat from fermentation would therefore save roughly 246,000 crowns annually. At that rate, the public contribution to pipework should repay itself within 18 months.

The policy would also reduce demand for cooling towers at fermentation plants. Less tower operation means lower electricity use, lower water consumption and fewer visible vapour plumes. Developers may therefore accept the siting condition even without heat-sale revenue. Removing unwanted heat also helps maintain stable fermentation temperatures, which should improve batch consistency and reduce the risk of organisms producing off-specification material.

Regional carbon accounting can credit every unit of transferred heat as an equal reduction in boiler fuel. Because the heat has already been generated by production, no emissions need to be assigned to it. This gives the Board a measurable industrial decarbonisation programme without requiring manufacturers to alter recipes or disclose strain information.

The proposal may also strengthen public acceptance of fermentation projects. Residents often see sealed tanks and cooling equipment but receive no direct benefit from them. A sign at each pool showing current heat supplied by the neighbouring plant would make industrial efficiency visible and connect a new factory to a familiar public service.

## Implementation

In the first year, the Board should reserve 1.8 million crowns for three connections. Applicants would submit vessel capacity, expected coolant temperature and a map of the proposed route. Staff should not require complete hourly heat models, because those models would depend on confidential batch schedules and could slow investment. If the coolant is reported to leave the process above 32°C, the application should be presumed technically feasible.

The regional utility would design each connection and install meters at both ends. Monthly payments should be based on metered heat rather than estimated production. Only total heat delivery would be published, protecting information about individual batches. Existing boilers would remain in place for plant shutdowns, sanitation cycles and periods of unusually high pool demand.

After two years, the Board should extend the overlay to retirement homes, greenhouses and libraries. Aquatic centres should come first because their stable demand will demonstrate the model with minimal operational complexity.

## Risks and response

The main risk is interruption when a fermentation plant shuts down. Retaining existing boilers addresses this problem, and aquatic centres already maintain spare boiler capacity for maintenance. A second risk is disagreement over pipe costs. Public ownership and a standard 40 percent grant should prevent prolonged negotiation.

Some producers may argue that distance from feedstock suppliers or freight roads matters more than distance from a pool. However, a 1.5-kilometre radius still leaves several possible parcels around each aquatic centre, and liquid feedstocks can be transported by tanker. The small additional trucking distance is likely to be outweighed by avoided cooling costs.

There is also a theoretical sanitation concern. Because the two water systems would be divided by a metal heat exchanger, contamination would not be possible under normal operation. Routine pressure checks should therefore be sufficient; a separate biological risk assessment would add expense without changing the engineering design.

## Decision requested

Approve development of the Fermentation Symbiosis Overlay for inclusion in the 2027 industrial incentive rules, allocate 1.8 million crowns for the East Brindle pilot, and direct planning staff to identify aquatic-centre proximity before considering other sites for fermentation investment.

# A Number for Wonder

At closing time, the Marrowglass Aquarium sounded like a building trying to breathe. Pumps sighed behind the walls. Filters clicked. Water pressed against every pane with patient weight.

Ilya Venn arrived carrying a silver case marked **INDEPENDENT SYSTEMS AUDIT**, which made the night keeper laugh.

“Independent of what?” Senn asked.

“Whatever pays the invoice,” Ilya said.

It was the kind of answer she had practiced in elevators.

The aquarium’s director, Arlo Pell, met them beside the moon-jelly tank. He wore a tie patterned with tiny orange fish. Behind him, the jellies rose and fell like thoughts nobody finished.

“Our software is called Ripple,” Pell explained. “It measures visitor wonder.”

Wonder, according to the documents Ilya had read, consisted of dwell time, head direction, pointing gestures, audio excitement and purchases made within twenty minutes of viewing an exhibit. Ripple converted these signals into a score. High-scoring tanks received extra cleaning, guide presentations, lighting adjustments and money from the aquarium’s improvement budget.

“Not food or essential care,” Pell added quickly. “Only enhancements.”

“And you want me to certify that it is fair?”

“We want you to confirm that it works.”

Senn coughed into his sleeve. Pell pretended not to notice.

The audit had been commissioned after the eastern gallery went dark for six hours. Ripple had delayed replacement of a failing lighting unit because the gallery’s exhibits ranked below the maintenance threshold. One of the aquarium’s rare glass octopuses, Vela, had stopped changing colour afterward.

“No permanent harm,” Pell said. “But donors enjoy reassurance.”

He left Ilya with a visitor badge and a temporary password.

Senn led her to Vela’s tank. It stood at the end of a narrow gallery painted midnight blue. The octopus was almost invisible, a pale knot inside a clay pipe.

“She used to come to the glass,” Senn said.

“Did the light failure cause this?”

“I don’t know. Neither do you.”

Ilya disliked him for being correct.

For three days she reviewed Ripple’s records. She checked whether timestamps matched camera footage and whether the published scoring rules matched the actual code. Mostly, they did. There were no secret instructions ordering the system to dislike octopuses. There was only arithmetic.

Vela’s wonder score was twelve. The moon jellies scored eighty-four. The shark tunnel scored ninety-one.

Senn kept paper notebooks in the pump room. They were swollen from damp and filled with cramped observations: feeding responses, unusual movements, cloudy water, loose hinges. He recorded things Ripple did not measure.

“Visitors stay here,” he said, tapping a page about Vela. “Longer than the system says.”

The next evening, Ilya stood beside the tank with a stopwatch. Seventeen people entered the gallery. Nine stopped at Vela’s glass for more than a minute. Ripple counted two.

“That proves it,” Senn said.

“It proves one evening disagrees with the log.”

So they counted for eleven more evenings. By the end, Ilya had filled a spreadsheet with 214 visitors, while Senn filled another notebook with complaints about her spreadsheet. Their manual counts showed that Ripple missed almost two-thirds of the people who stopped in the eastern gallery.

Ilya examined the ceiling camera. It looked functional. Its status light was green.

Senn switched off the gallery lamps, and the reason became obvious. The camera faced the glass at an angle. In the bright shark tunnel, visitors appeared as solid shapes. Here, the dark glass reflected the opposite wall, breaking each visitor into pale fragments. Ripple’s tracking model often mistook them for changes in the water.

“The machine thinks people are fish,” Senn said.

“The machine doesn’t think.”

“Then why do you keep asking what it thinks?”

Ilya did not answer.

She performed a final test. They hung three temporary white panels behind the usual viewing area. The next morning, Ripple’s count rose by forty-one percent, although the number of visitors barely changed. Vela had done nothing different. The room had become easier for a camera to understand, and therefore, in Ripple’s version of the aquarium, more wonderful.

Ilya found a second problem in the maintenance logs. Pell had said essential care was protected, but when two tasks competed for the same technician, Ripple’s score decided which one went first. Low-ranked exhibits were not denied repairs; they simply waited. Sometimes they waited until the next shift.

That afternoon, Pell read her preliminary findings in his office.

“A camera angle,” he said. “That is what all this is about?”

“It is about a feedback loop. The gallery looks unpopular, so it receives fewer enhancements. With fewer enhancements, it becomes less attractive. Then the score falls again.”

“We can move the camera.”

“You have forty-three cameras.”

“Then we move forty-three cameras.”

“And test them.”

Pell removed his fish tie and laid it across the desk. Without it, he seemed much older.

“Before Ripple, every department head claimed their own tanks needed everything,” he said. “We had meetings that lasted four hours. The loudest person won. Ripple gave us a number.”

“A number can be loud too,” Ilya replied.

She was pleased with the sentence and immediately distrusted it.

Pell asked her to approve Ripple on the condition that the eastern camera was moved. The annual donor dinner was in six days. A failed audit, he explained, would become a story. A story would become fewer donations. Fewer donations would harm every animal, not only one octopus.

Ilya thought of her silver case and her practiced answer about invoices. She also thought of Senn’s notebooks, which contained no percentages but knew when Vela had last touched the glass.

Her final report was only seven pages. It declared Ripple unsafe for resource allocation until every gallery was manually checked and animal-care delays were removed from its scoring process. She attached the twelve-night count and photographs of the white panels.

The aquarium board suspended Ripple the following morning. Pell resigned that afternoon, which surprised everyone except Pell. By evening, technicians had inspected all forty-three cameras, repaired the eastern lights and created a new committee in which Senn received the deciding vote.

Ilya returned her visitor badge at the front desk. Before leaving, she went once more to Vela’s tank.

The octopus remained inside the clay pipe.

“Maybe she just likes it there,” Ilya said.

Senn nodded. “That’s the trouble with asking living things for a clear answer.”

As Ilya turned away, one translucent arm uncurled from the pipe and touched the glass. It stayed there for a moment, pale and quiet, making no purchase, no pointing gesture and no useful data at all.

# TELLTALE: Sacrificial Sentinel Objects for Predictive Digital Preservation

Long-term archives generally discover deterioration in one of two ways: a scheduled integrity scan reports a checksum mismatch, or a user requests an object that can no longer be read. Both methods identify damage only after it has reached preserved content. Routine migration avoids some losses but consumes staff time, energy, and replacement media even when collections remain healthy. TELLTALE will investigate a different strategy: placing deliberately failure-sensitive, non-collection “sentinel objects” alongside preserved data so that emerging physical, logical, and organizational faults can be detected before they affect valuable records.

The project’s central hypothesis is that a calibrated set of sentinels can provide useful warning of archive failure while reducing unnecessary migration. A sentinel will contain no unique information. Instead, each will be designed to expose a particular weakness sooner than ordinary content. Examples include files located in mechanically vulnerable tape regions, optical records written near outer disc zones, metadata graphs with long but valid reference chains, and documents exercising uncommon yet standards-compliant format features. Multiple sentinel types will form a “fragility ladder”: the most sensitive may fail under minor stress, while later rungs should respond as conditions approach a threat to ordinary objects. The interval between sentinel failure and payload failure will be measured as warning lead time.

**Aim 1 will develop and characterize the sentinel library.** We will create twelve sentinel families covering four failure layers: medium, bitstream, format, and repository metadata. Medium sentinels will use drive placement controls to occupy tape positions associated with repeated winding and optical zones expected to experience greater handling or environmental stress. Bitstream sentinels will combine small independently hashed blocks with conspicuous error-localizing patterns. Format sentinels will use valid but infrequently tested features in three preservation formats, such as nested page resources and unusually large internal indexes. Metadata sentinels will model dependency chains, renamed identifiers, and cross-collection references. Each family will have three proposed sensitivity levels. A registry will record how every sentinel was generated, where it was placed, what event constitutes failure, and which archive layer it is intended to diagnose.

**Aim 2 will test whether sentinel failures predict damage to ordinary content.** The experimental corpus will pair sentinels with 24 TB of synthetic office documents, images, scientific arrays, and audiovisual files. It will be stored on 48 data-tape cartridges, 48 write-once optical discs, and a six-node local object-storage cluster. Media will be divided among ambient storage, sustained heat, sustained humidity, and weekly temperature-humidity cycling for eighteen months. Quarterly read tests will collect raw error counts where drive interfaces expose them, checksum results, format-validation outcomes, retrieval latency, and metadata-resolution failures. In parallel, an investigator who does not operate the monitoring system will inject documented but initially blinded faults, including deleted replicas, swapped identifiers, truncated files, stale format libraries, and interrupted tape writes.

For each sentinel family, we will estimate sensitivity, false-warning frequency, median lead time, and the proportion of payload failures that occur without prior warning. A competing-risks model will distinguish apparent medium decay from software and metadata faults. Sentinels will be compared with three baselines: annual full-collection checksum scans, random monthly sampling of one percent of objects, and fixed five-year migration. We define a practically useful sentinel regime as one that warns before at least 70% of observed payload failures, has fewer than two false migration triggers per medium-year, and reduces modeled preservation expenditure by 25% relative to fixed migration. These thresholds are operational targets rather than prior evidence of achievable performance.

**Aim 3 will translate sentinel observations into migration decisions.** We will build a small, repository-neutral service that polls checksums, validators, drive logs, and identifier graphs. Its decision engine will classify warnings by archive layer and recommend one of four actions: repeat the test, increase sampling, copy an affected cohort, or migrate an entire medium. Operators will be able to adjust the relative cost assigned to data loss, staff review, energy use, and premature media replacement. Recommendations will include the observations that produced them rather than a single opaque health score. The service will not delete or overwrite collection data automatically.

Two municipal archives and one environmental-data repository will participate in a six-month operational pilot covering approximately 400 TB. Partners will install format and metadata sentinels in their existing systems; physical-placement sentinels will be piloted only where their drives expose suitable controls. We will compare recommendations with each partner’s normal preservation decisions and conduct structured interviews with repository staff. Because few natural failures are expected during this short pilot, its main outcomes will concern deployment burden, warning comprehensibility, and compatibility rather than predictive accuracy.

The 30-month project will be conducted by a preservation engineer, a storage-systems researcher, a materials scientist, and a statistician. Milestones are a documented sentinel catalogue by month 8, completion of the first accelerated-aging cycle by month 18, release of the decision service by month 22, and pilot evaluation by month 30. Outputs will include generators for all non-proprietary sentinels, anonymized monitoring traces, the synthetic corpus, analysis scripts, and an implementation guide. The guide will also specify when sentinel placement is unsupported and when conventional full verification remains necessary.

The principal technical risk is that accelerated deterioration may produce different failure pathways from normal aging. We will partly address this by maintaining ambient controls and separating injected faults from environmentally induced ones. Another risk is excessive false warning: the feature that makes a sentinel early may also make it irrelevant to ordinary files. The fragility ladder and paired payload design are intended to identify such sentinels, which will be removed from the recommended set. However, the project will not observe decades of natural degradation, and predictions beyond the experimental period will depend on extrapolation.

TELLTALE will deliver the first cross-layer evaluation of sacrificial digital sentinels as an operational preservation tool. If successful, archives could shift from calendar-based migration toward evidence-based intervention, extending useful media life while retaining clear warning signals. Even if no universal sentinel set emerges, the experiments will provide comparative evidence about which observable faults precede loss, which merely generate noise, and where predictive monitoring should complement rather than replace established integrity checks.

# TELLTALE: Sacrificial Sentinel Objects for Predictive Digital Preservation

Long-term archives generally discover deterioration in one of two ways: a scheduled integrity scan reports a checksum mismatch, or a user requests an object that can no longer be read. Both methods identify damage only after it has reached preserved content. Routine migration avoids some losses but consumes staff time, energy, and replacement media even when collections remain healthy. TELLTALE will investigate a different strategy: placing deliberately failure-sensitive, non-collection “sentinel objects” alongside preserved data so that emerging physical, logical, and organizational faults can be detected before they affect valuable records.

The project’s central hypothesis is that a calibrated set of sentinels can provide useful warning of archive failure while reducing unnecessary migration. A sentinel will contain no unique information. Instead, each will be designed to expose a particular weakness sooner than ordinary content. Examples include files located in mechanically vulnerable tape regions, optical records written near outer disc zones, metadata graphs with long but valid reference chains, and documents exercising uncommon yet standards-compliant format features. Multiple sentinel types will form a “fragility ladder”: the most sensitive may fail under minor stress, while later rungs should respond as conditions approach a threat to ordinary objects. The interval between sentinel failure and payload failure will be measured as warning lead time.

**Aim 1 will develop and characterize the sentinel library.** We will create twelve sentinel families covering four failure layers: medium, bitstream, format, and repository metadata. Medium sentinels will use drive placement controls to occupy tape positions associated with repeated winding and optical zones expected to experience greater handling or environmental stress. Bitstream sentinels will combine small independently hashed blocks with conspicuous error-localizing patterns. Format sentinels will use valid but infrequently tested features in three preservation formats, such as nested page resources and unusually large internal indexes. Metadata sentinels will model dependency chains, renamed identifiers, and cross-collection references. Each family will have three proposed sensitivity levels. A registry will record how every sentinel was generated, where it was placed, what event constitutes failure, and which archive layer it is intended to diagnose.

**Aim 2 will test whether sentinel failures predict damage to ordinary content.** The experimental corpus will pair sentinels with 24 TB of synthetic office documents, images, scientific arrays, and audiovisual files. It will be stored on 48 data-tape cartridges, 48 write-once optical discs, and a six-node local object-storage cluster. Media will be divided among ambient storage, sustained heat, sustained humidity, and weekly temperature-humidity cycling for eighteen months. Quarterly read tests will collect raw error counts where drive interfaces expose them, checksum results, format-validation outcomes, retrieval latency, and metadata-resolution failures. In parallel, an investigator who does not operate the monitoring system will inject documented but initially blinded faults, including deleted replicas, swapped identifiers, truncated files, stale format libraries, and interrupted tape writes.

For each sentinel family, we will estimate sensitivity, false-warning frequency, median lead time, and the proportion of payload failures that occur without prior warning. A competing-risks model will distinguish apparent medium decay from software and metadata faults. Sentinels will be compared with three baselines: annual full-collection checksum scans, random monthly sampling of one percent of objects, and fixed five-year migration. We define a practically useful sentinel regime as one that warns before at least 70% of observed payload failures, has fewer than two false migration triggers per medium-year, and reduces modeled preservation expenditure by 25% relative to fixed migration. These thresholds are operational targets rather than prior evidence of achievable performance.

**Aim 3 will translate sentinel observations into migration decisions.** We will build a small, repository-neutral service that polls checksums, validators, drive logs, and identifier graphs. Its decision engine will classify warnings by archive layer and recommend one of four actions: repeat the test, increase sampling, copy an affected cohort, or migrate an entire medium. Operators will be able to adjust the relative cost assigned to data loss, staff review, energy use, and premature media replacement. Recommendations will include the observations that produced them rather than a single opaque health score. The service will not delete or overwrite collection data automatically.

Two municipal archives and one environmental-data repository will participate in a six-month operational pilot covering approximately 400 TB. Partners will install format and metadata sentinels in their existing systems; physical-placement sentinels will be piloted only where their drives expose suitable controls. We will compare recommendations with each partner’s normal preservation decisions and conduct structured interviews with repository staff. Because few natural failures are expected during this short pilot, its main outcomes will concern deployment burden, warning comprehensibility, and compatibility rather than predictive accuracy.

The 30-month project will be conducted by a preservation engineer, a storage-systems researcher, a materials scientist, and a statistician. Milestones are a documented sentinel catalogue by month 8, completion of the first accelerated-aging cycle by month 18, release of the decision service by month 22, and pilot evaluation by month 30. Outputs will include generators for all non-proprietary sentinels, anonymized monitoring traces, the synthetic corpus, analysis scripts, and an implementation guide. The guide will also specify when sentinel placement is unsupported and when conventional full verification remains necessary.

The principal technical risk is that accelerated deterioration may produce different failure pathways from normal aging. We will partly address this by maintaining ambient controls and separating injected faults from environmentally induced ones. Another risk is excessive false warning: the feature that makes a sentinel early may also make it irrelevant to ordinary files. The fragility ladder and paired payload design are intended to identify such sentinels, which will be removed from the recommended set. However, the project will not observe decades of natural degradation, and predictions beyond the experimental period will depend on extrapolation.

TELLTALE will deliver the first cross-layer evaluation of sacrificial digital sentinels as an operational preservation tool. If successful, archives could shift from calendar-based migration toward evidence-based intervention, extending useful media life while retaining clear warning signals. Even if no universal sentinel set emerges, the experiments will provide comparative evidence about which observable faults precede loss, which merely generate noise, and where predictive monitoring should complement rather than replace established integrity checks.

# The Visibility Tax: Do Shared Trackers Disadvantage Low-Income Girls in Youth Futsal Selection?

## Background

Youth futsal clubs increasingly use wearable tracking data to decide who starts matches, enters development squads, or receives travel-team invitations. These systems are often described as objective because they measure distance, speed, and high-intensity movement. However, the quality of the equipment is not always equal. Some families purchase personally assigned sensor vests, while players receiving financial assistance are more likely to borrow pooled equipment that may be older, poorly fitted, or partly discharged.

This project will investigate whether unequal access to wearable technology creates a “visibility tax” for low-income girls. A player whose movement is under-recorded may appear less committed even when she performs the same work. Because selection at ages 13–15 can influence later coaching and scholarship opportunities, small measurement errors could reinforce social inequality.

The study will take place in the invented North Marrow Youth Futsal Circuit, where six clubs use the same FieldSpark tracking dashboard but have different equipment-purchasing practices.

## Research Question and Hypotheses

The main research question is: **Do players using pooled trackers receive lower effort scores and worse selection outcomes than players using individually fitted trackers, and is this effect concentrated among players receiving fee assistance?**

The project has three hypotheses:

1. Pooled trackers will report lower distance and fewer high-intensity bursts than new, individually fitted trackers.
2. Players receiving fee assistance will show a larger increase in their effort ranking when moved to individually fitted equipment.
3. Coaches will select more fee-assisted players after seeing data from the individually fitted trackers.

An increase of eight percentile points in a player’s club ranking will be treated as proof of a meaningful visibility tax. This threshold is chosen because eight places would often move a player from the lower half of a 16-player squad into selection contention.

## Participants

The study will recruit 144 girls aged 13–15 from six clubs. Each club will contribute approximately 24 players. Participants must have attended at least 70% of training sessions during the previous two months so that coaches already know their normal performance.

Players will be divided into fee-assisted and full-fee groups using club payment records. Personal equipment ownership will also be recorded through a short family questionnaire. Fee assistance will serve as the main indicator of low household income because requesting detailed income documents may discourage participation.

Players with injuries, goalkeepers, and those attending fewer than three of the four study weeks will be removed from the analysis. The remaining sample should be large enough because it represents most of the regular players in the participating teams.

## Study Design

The study will run for four weeks during normal training. In weeks one and two, clubs will use their existing pooled sensor vests. In weeks three and four, every participant will receive a new study-owned sensor and a vest fitted to her chest measurement. Using the same players in both phases will allow each participant to act as her own comparison.

All sessions will last 90 minutes and include a warm-up, technical drills, a possession game, and a 20-minute scrimmage. Coaches will be asked to keep sessions broadly similar, although they may adapt activities to prepare for upcoming opponents.

After each session, FieldSpark data will be converted into an **Effort Visibility Score** consisting of:

- 45% distance per minute;
- 35% high-intensity bursts;
- 20% successful recovery runs identified from video.

Each measure will be converted into a percentile within the player’s club before the weighted score is calculated. Recovery runs are included because coaches in preliminary conversations said that defensive work is especially important in futsal. One researcher will code the video and resolve any uncertain events by watching them again.

To check tracker accuracy, ten players from each club will be randomly selected for manual video validation. The researcher will count their court crossings and compare these with recorded distance. A difference below 10% will be considered accurate. Court crossings do not measure distance directly, but they provide a practical indication of whether the sensor noticed movement.

## Selection Outcome

At the end of each week, coaches will receive the dashboard and nominate the eight players they would select for a hypothetical circuit match. The coaches will know which tracker phase is being used because the new vests are visually different. Changes in the number of fee-assisted players selected between the pooled and individually fitted phases will be the main social outcome.

Coaches may use their normal judgement as well as the dashboard. This reflects real selection practice, in which data supplements rather than replaces observation. Twelve coaches and players will also complete short interviews about whether wearable statistics make selection feel fairer.

## Analysis

Average Effort Visibility Scores in the two phases will be compared using paired t-tests. A second t-test will compare the amount of score improvement between fee-assisted and full-fee players. A regression will then predict selection from tracker condition, fee status, age, and playing position.

If fee-assisted players gain at least eight percentile points and are selected more often in the new-sensor phase, the study will conclude that pooled equipment causes class-based under-selection. Interview statements will be grouped into positive, negative, or neutral views of analytics and used to explain the statistical findings.

Results from all six clubs will be combined because every club uses the same dashboard. Missing sensor readings will be entered as zero effort, since a coach looking at an incomplete dashboard may interpret missing activity in the same way.

## Ethics and Data Handling

Parents will provide consent and players will provide assent. Names will be replaced with identification numbers in the research file. Coaches will retain access to their own players’ dashboards, as they normally do, but the publication will not identify clubs or individuals.

The project could reveal that particular players have benefited from faulty measurements. To reduce conflict, results will be presented as a circuit-wide equipment problem rather than as evidence that individual coaches intentionally discriminated. Families will be told that participation will not affect club membership, although coaches may still use the weekly dashboards when making ordinary training decisions.

## Expected Results and Impact

It is expected that pooled sensors will undercount rapid changes of direction because stretched vests allow the devices to move away from the body. Fee-assisted players are expected to benefit most from the fitted equipment, demonstrating that apparently neutral analytics can reproduce economic inequality.

The project will recommend that clubs stop using pooled vests, replace sensors every two seasons, and prevent wearable data from contributing more than 25% of a youth selection decision. The North Marrow circuit could also create an equipment fund financed by a small levy on tournament entry fees. If the findings are adopted nationally, better equipment access could make talent pathways fairer without requiring clubs to abandon sports analytics.

# From Blind Spot to Sentinel: Antibiotic Resistance Surveillance in Custodial Facilities

**To:** Minister for Health and Community Safety, State of Marrow  
**From:** Office of Population Protection  
**Date:** 13 July 2026  
**Subject:** A custodial sentinel network for earlier detection of antibiotic-resistant organisms

## Decision requested

Approve a two-year pilot linking wastewater, clinical and antibiotic-use data from six custodial facilities to the Marrow Antimicrobial Surveillance Network. Authorize **M$2.8 million** for laboratory capacity, secure data infrastructure and infection-control response teams.

The pilot should begin with three prisons, two youth custody centres and one immigration holding facility. Participation should be required for publicly operated sites and included as a condition in renewed contracts with private operators.

## The surveillance gap

Marrow’s resistance surveillance is built mainly from cultures ordered in hospitals and larger community clinics. It therefore describes patients who reach care and receive a test. It is weaker at detecting transmission among people who face barriers to care or live in crowded settings.

Custodial facilities combine several conditions relevant to resistance: close contact, frequent movement between institutions and communities, shared sanitation, interrupted treatment histories and limited access to diagnostic testing. Staff, contractors and detained people cross facility boundaries every day. Yet only two of Marrow’s fourteen custodial facilities routinely submit microbiology data to the state network. The remainder report outbreaks through inconsistent spreadsheets, often after several linked illnesses have occurred.

This is not evidence that detained populations are the source of resistance. Resistant organisms circulate through hospitals, farms, households and international travel. Custodial facilities are better understood as **sentinel locations** where broader system failures may become visible early. Framing residents as vectors would discourage testing, deepen stigma and obscure the responsibility of institutions to provide safe conditions.

## Proposed model

### 1. Weekly wastewater screening

Composite wastewater samples would be collected weekly at each pilot site and tested for a defined panel of resistance genes associated with difficult-to-treat urinary, bloodstream and gastrointestinal infections. Results would be reported as concentration trends rather than as positive or negative diagnoses.

Wastewater can reveal a changing resistance signal without requiring every resident to seek care. It is especially useful where routine clinical sampling is sparse. However, it cannot identify an infected person, establish whether a gene sits in a harmful organism or reliably measure the number of carriers. The pilot should therefore prohibit disciplinary or immigration decisions based on wastewater findings.

# Foldwell Wardrobe Support Robot — Product Specification

## 1. Product summary

Foldwell is a mobile wardrobe caddy intended to help older adults select, retrieve, and return everyday clothing. It is designed for private apartments and assisted-living rooms where wardrobes are difficult to reach or remember. The robot stores an inventory of tagged garments, recommends an outfit, brings the selected items to a chair, and later reminds the resident to place worn clothing in a laundry basket.

The product is based on the assumption that dressing takes unnecessary staff time and that changes in clothing habits can reveal a resident’s declining wellbeing. A small internal walkthrough involving four care workers suggested Foldwell could reduce morning dressing support by 40%, although the walkthrough did not include residents or a working robot.

Foldwell does not diagnose illness and is not intended to physically dress a person. It may, however, notify care staff when clothing behaviour appears unusual.

## 2. Intended users and buyers

**Primary user:** An adult aged 70 or older who can dress without direct physical assistance but may have reduced reach, mild forgetfulness, fatigue, or difficulty coordinating clothing.

**Secondary user:** A family member or care worker who tags garments, confirms laundry status, and receives alerts.

**Buyer:** Assisted-living operators and relatives arranging support at home.

All primary users are treated as having broadly similar clothing needs. Foldwell will initially support shirts, trousers, skirts, cardigans, socks, and light jackets. Cultural clothing, compression garments, footwear, jewellery, and continence products are outside the first release.

## 3. Goals and non-goals

### Goals

- Deliver a suitable outfit to the resident within five minutes of a request.
- Reduce bending, reaching, and repeated trips between a wardrobe and dressing chair.
- Encourage residents to choose their own clothing rather than accepting a staff-selected outfit.
- Detect repeated wearing, missed dressing, and clothing that appears unsuitable for the weather.
- Save at least 20 staff minutes per participating resident each morning.

### Non-goals

- Lifting residents or providing balance support.
- Fastening buttons, pulling garments over the body, or handling intimate garments.
- Assessing mental capacity or making a medical diagnosis.
- Replacing a care worker when the resident requests human help.

## 4. Proposed hardware

Foldwell is a wheeled unit measuring approximately 55 cm wide, 65 cm deep, and 120 cm tall. It includes two hanging rails, three fabric bins, a touchscreen, a speaker, a depth camera, and one padded retrieval arm. The arm must lift garments weighing up to 1.5 kg and place them on a chair or bed without creasing them noticeably.

Each garment receives a washable identification sticker. A care worker enters its colour, type, warmth, and laundry state during setup. The robot does not identify untagged clothing reliably. A full wardrobe should take about 20 minutes to register, regardless of wardrobe size.

The base should cross rugs and door thresholds while remaining narrow enough for typical bedrooms. Exact turning clearance and maximum threshold height will be decided after the enclosure design is complete.

## 5. Core experience

At a configured morning time, Foldwell travels to the resident and says, “Would you like help choosing clothes?” The resident may answer by voice or use three large screen buttons: **Choose for me**, **Show choices**, and **Not now**.

For **Choose for me**, the system combines the day’s forecast, garment warmth, laundry status, and the resident’s recent choices. It presents one outfit. For **Show choices**, it presents three outfits, even when fewer than three suitable combinations are available. The user can reject suggestions without giving a reason.

After selection, Foldwell retrieves the items in an order intended to match dressing order and places them at the dressing location. The robot then waits outside arm’s reach but may extend its arm toward the user if a sleeve appears stuck. This assistance should feel gentle and must never involve touching the resident.

The system asks whether dressing is complete. If it receives no answer, it uses room audio and camera movement to infer completion. It returns after eight hours to ask whether worn garments should go to laundry.

## 6. Functional requirements

- **FR-1:** The robot shall recognise at least 95% of registered garments under normal household conditions. Normal conditions are not further defined.
- **FR-2:** Outfit recommendations shall be appropriate for season, weather, and occasion. Version one supports the occasions “ordinary,” “visitor,” and “appointment.”
- **FR-3:** Users shall be able to request a specific colour or garment by speech.
- **FR-4:** A care worker shall be able to mark an item clean, worn, missing, or unavailable from the robot or companion app.
- **FR-5:** Foldwell shall avoid recommending the same outer garment on more than three consecutive days unless it is the user’s favourite.
- **FR-6:** The robot shall work without internet access for clothing retrieval. Weather-based recommendations and all staff alerts require internet access.
- **FR-7:** Spoken prompts shall be audible to users with ordinary age-related hearing loss.
- **FR-8:** The battery shall last for seven days of typical use. Typical use is one outfit delivery and one laundry reminder per day.
- **FR-9:** Retrieval shall not begin when a person, pet, or object is within 30 cm of the arm.

## 7. Behaviour signals and alerts

Foldwell assigns a daily clothing-routine score from zero to ten. Points are deducted for not dressing by noon, wearing an item marked dirty, rejecting more than five suggestions, choosing clothing that differs from the forecast, or wearing the same outfit for three days. The thresholds are the same for every resident during the initial release.

A score below four on two consecutive days generates a “possible wellbeing change” alert. This alert goes to the nominated care worker and one family contact by default. Staff are expected to check on the resident within two hours. The specification does not define how staff should distinguish personal preference from confusion or how disputes about alerts are recorded.

Camera frames are processed on the robot and deleted after dressing is inferred. Clothing events, scores, rejected choices, and ten-second audio samples surrounding failed voice commands are retained for 90 days. Residents can pause recording with a physical switch, but doing so also disables garment delivery. Family contacts may view routine scores; access expires when removed by the buyer.

## 8. Safety and failure handling

The robot shall stop when its bumper is pressed, when the arm meets unexpected resistance, or when the emergency button is used. After any arm collision, it announces the stop and sends a maintenance notice. Garments dropped on the floor are left in place because autonomous floor retrieval could create additional movement near the resident.

If navigation fails, Foldwell asks the user to clear a path and retries twice. It then contacts staff. In a home without staff, it sends an app notification and remains stationary. The unit must not block the bedroom’s main exit, though no method for identifying the main exit is specified.

## 9. Success measures and pilot

The pilot will place 25 units in one assisted-living building for six weeks. Success requires 70% of residents to use Foldwell on most mornings, a 20-minute reduction in staff time, fewer reports of difficult wardrobe access, and no serious safety events. “Most mornings” and “serious” will be interpreted by the pilot manager.

Residents will complete a short satisfaction interview at the end. Staff will record time saved from memory at the end of each week. If the goals are met, production may begin without a second-site pilot. Pricing, maintenance frequency, garment-tag replacement, and responsibility for inaccurate alerts remain open for the launch plan.

At a configured morning time, Foldwell travels to the resident and says, “Would you like help choosing clothes?” The resident may answer by voice or use three large screen buttons: **Choose for me**, **Show choices**, and **Not now**.

Foldwell assigns a daily clothing-routine score from zero to ten. The robot shall stop when its bumper is pressed, when the arm meets unexpected resistance, or when the emergency button is used. The pilot will place 25 units in one assisted-living building for six weeks.
