# Policy Memorandum: ShelfRoute Surplus Food Collection

**To:** City Manager and Belden Quay Municipal Cabinet  
**From:** Office of Circular Services  
**Date:** 13 July 2026  
**Subject:** Using library transfer vans and branch return rooms to recover commercial food surplus

## Decision requested

Approve a twelve-month, citywide initiative called **ShelfRoute**, under which the Belden Quay Library Service will collect surplus food from participating shops during its existing interbranch transfer rounds. Food will be consolidated in library return rooms and offered through unattended community lockers at selected branches.

The requested first-year appropriation is **$311,000**, including equipment, locker installation, communications, and a contingency. ShelfRoute is expected to recover 1,500 tonnes of food in its first year, equivalent to approximately 3.6 million meals. The program would use no additional vehicles and only limited additional staff time. On that basis, its social return would exceed $25 million, and its direct waste-disposal savings would cover most annual operating costs after the installation year.

The Cabinet should approve the full network rather than a small pilot. A pilot would delay food recovery and would not test the route density on which the program depends. The first eight weeks of citywide operation can serve as an adjustment period, with locker locations or collection times changed as evidence emerges.

## The problem

Belden Quay sends edible food to disposal while running municipal vehicles on partially empty return journeys. These problems are usually managed separately: waste officers encourage businesses to separate organics, social services purchase food assistance, and the library moves books among branches. ShelfRoute combines them into one logistics system.

The Office of Circular Services conducted an eleven-day observation of four businesses on Alder Row: a bakery, a small supermarket, a noodle shop, and a hotel café. Staff weighed food placed in refuse or organics bins at closing. The four businesses discarded 612 kilograms, of which observers judged 71 percent to be edible at the time it entered the bin. Bread, uncut fruit, packaged salads, prepared noodles, and sealed yogurt made up most of the edible portion.

If the average from these four businesses is multiplied by the city’s 1,370 registered food premises and 365 days, commercial premises discard about 19,000 tonnes of edible food each year. This calculation assumes that the observed businesses are representative. The hotel café was larger than most premises, but the bakery was smaller, so the difference probably balances out. Even if the estimate is twice the true amount, recovering 1,500 tonnes would require capturing less than one-sixth of available surplus.

Businesses interviewed during the observation gave three reasons for not donating more food:

1. Charities collect at inconvenient or unpredictable times.
2. A small quantity at one shop does not justify a dedicated vehicle trip.
3. Staff do not know which organization will accept each product.

These are logistics barriers rather than a shortage of goodwill. All four managers said they would place food in a standardized crate if collection occurred near closing and required less than five minutes. None would pay for a separate collection, although two said they might accept a small reduction in their commercial waste bill.

The city already operates an underused collection network. Six library transfer vans circulate among 21 branches and the Central Collections Building. They carry reserved books, returns, exhibition materials, and internal mail. Fleet sheets show that vans are 74 percent full when leaving the central building but only 38 percent full on their final inward legs. The available space is in the right general direction: neighborhood branches are near food businesses, and the final legs converge on central or district facilities.

ShelfRoute would therefore turn empty return capacity into a public food asset without creating another fleet.

## Proposed operating model

### 1. Businesses pack surplus into ShelfCrates

Participating businesses would receive stackable, lidded containers in three colors:

- **Yellow:** bread, pastries, and dry packaged food;
- **Green:** whole fruit and vegetables;
- **Blue:** chilled prepared food and sealed dairy products.

Each business would print a label showing the product name, packing time, allergens, and intended locker destination. A simple web form would generate both the label and a collection notice. Businesses without a printer could write the same information on a supplied card.

The first eight weeks would accept only yellow and green crates. Blue crates would be added once branch staff are familiar with the process. Raw meat, raw fish, alcohol, food from customer plates, damaged cans, and products visibly affected by mold would never be eligible. This exclusion is simple enough for shop staff to remember.

Donors would decide whether an item is fit to offer. Requiring city staff to inspect every product would slow collection and make the city appear to assume ownership of the food. Branch staff would check that lids are closed and labels are present but would not open containers.

### 2. Businesses bring crates to a nearby branch

A business would select a participating library branch within 800 metres and deliver its crate between 4:00 p.m. and branch closing. This is preferable to asking vans to stop at each shop. The city would still call the service a collection program because the municipal network performs the long-distance movement.

An 800-metre distance should be short enough for a staff member to walk with a wheeled crate. The Alder Row bakery already sends an employee approximately 600 metres to deposit daily banking, suggesting that comparable trips can fit within closing duties. Businesses farther from a branch could ask a neighboring shop to carry their crate or could participate only on days when an employee is driving past a library.

At the branch, crates would be placed in the book-return sorting room. These rooms are secure, have washable floors, and are generally cooler than retail kitchens because they are not used for cooking. Food crates would occupy a marked zone separated from books by floor tape. A lid provides the main barrier, so constructing separate rooms is unnecessary.

### 3. Existing transfer vans move consolidated crates

The library’s evening van schedule would be amended as follows:

| Transfer loop | Current final movement | ShelfRoute use | Expected added time |
|---|---|---|---:|
| North Arc | 5 branches to Central Collections | Collect yellow and green crates | 22 minutes |
| Harbor Bend | 4 branches to Wren District Library | Collect all crate types after week 8 | 18 minutes |
| East Ladder | 5 branches to Central Collections | Collect yellow and green crates | 26 minutes |
| South Pair | 3 branches to Oriole Branch | Collect all crate types after week 8 | 14 minutes |
| Hill Spur | 2 branches to Central Collections | Collection on Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday | 9 minutes |
| Civic Loop | Central Collections to administrative offices | Carry empty, cleaned crates outward | 12 minutes |

The estimates assume two minutes to load each participating branch. Drivers already stop at the branches, so additional time consists mostly of rolling crates between the building and van. The cumulative added time is not expected to create overtime because routes regularly finish before the end of scheduled shifts. The library has not supplied route-by-route records of early finishes, but supervisors describe 20 to 45 minutes of ordinary variation.

Food would travel in the same cargo compartment as books but in lidded containers. Blue crates would be wrapped in reusable insulated covers. Vans would not need mechanical refrigeration because each journey is under 90 minutes and Belden Quay’s average evening temperature is below 18 degrees Celsius for most of the year. On unusually warm days, branches could place blue crates near an air-conditioning vent until loading.

### 4. Food enters branch lockers or community distribution

Twelve branches would receive banks of six lockers. Yellow and green crates arriving at Central Collections would be sorted by destination and sent back out the following morning. Blue crates would go directly to lockers on the same evening where possible. A local community organization could also reserve a full crate through the ShelfRoute portal.

Locker users would register with a phone number and receive a four-digit code. No income test would apply. An income test would create paperwork, embarrass users, and leave food unclaimed. Each account could open two lockers per week during the first month. The limit could later be raised if supplies are abundant.

A locker listing would describe the food but would not guarantee an exact quantity. For example, a listing might state “mixed bread and pastries, approximately one shopping bag.” This allows volunteers to fill lockers quickly. Food not claimed within 24 hours would be moved to organics collection. Because the aim is to rescue food, an unclaimed rate below 40 percent should count as acceptable in the launch period.

The locker banks would not be refrigerated. The program would reserve them primarily for bread, produce, and packaged shelf-stable goods. Blue-crate food would be placed only in lockers located inside air-conditioned vestibules and would carry a same-evening collection instruction. A text message would tell the user when the item was loaded, making the recipient responsible for timely collection.

## Why the library network is the preferred carrier

Three alternatives were considered.

### Dedicated refrigerated collection

A purpose-built service would offer greater control over temperatures and pickup times. Preliminary fleet prices indicate that three refrigerated vans, charging equipment, drivers, and a depot would cost at least $1.2 million in the first year. This option is disproportionate when the city already has vans visiting the same neighborhoods.

### Grants to charities

The city could fund existing food groups to expand collections. This would preserve their expertise and relationships with recipients. However, each group has its own intake rules, and several operate only two or three days per week. Giving grants would not automatically create a unified network. It would also be difficult to determine whether the city had purchased additional collections or merely subsidized trips that would have happened anyway.

### Library-based reverse logistics

The library network has fixed routes, public buildings, trusted neighborhood locations, and unused return capacity. It is the only option that solves consolidation, transport, and public access at once. Library branches also attract people for ordinary reasons, so a resident collecting food does not have to enter a building identified solely with assistance.

The principal objection is that carrying food is outside the library’s mission. That view is too narrow. Libraries already move objects, maintain reservations, issue user codes, and operate neighborhood service points. ShelfRoute applies those capabilities to a different item. A crate of bread is operationally similar to a crate of books because both need a label, a destination, and dry handling.

## Expected quantities and financial case

ShelfRoute’s first-year target is 1,500 tonnes. The target can be reached if 450 businesses provide an average of 9.1 kilograms per operating day. The four observed businesses each discarded an average of 13.9 kilograms per day, so the target includes a margin for missed days and ineligible products.

Nine kilograms is roughly one crate. Therefore, the daily network would handle about 450 crates. The six vans can each carry 75 crates in their currently unused space, producing exactly 450 crates of daily capacity. This calculation does not account for differences between the external dimensions of bakery crates, produce crates, and library totes, but the proposed ShelfCrate is designed to stack.

A typical crate will not always weigh nine kilograms. Bread crates may weigh only three kilograms, while produce crates could weigh 15 kilograms. Lighter crates would reduce recovered tonnage but allow more units per van. Heavier crates would increase tonnage without increasing the number of loading movements. For planning purposes, these effects can be treated as offsetting.

Estimated first-year costs are:

| Item | Cost |
|---|---:|
| 600 ShelfCrates and wheeled carriers | $67,000 |
| 12 locker banks, wiring, and installation | $106,000 |
| Label and reservation portal | $38,000 |
| Cleaning supplies and insulated covers | $19,000 |
| Business recruitment and printed guidance | $21,000 |
| Library staff training | $7,000 |
| Additional fuel and vehicle cleaning | $13,000 |
| Contingency | $40,000 |
| **Total** | **$311,000** |

No driver or branch staffing line is included. The work would be absorbed into existing shifts. Loading is estimated to add 101 minutes across six routes each evening, or less than 17 minutes per driver. Branch employees would spend about four minutes accepting and logging each crate, but this would be spread across 21 sites and should resemble the time already spent handling complex book returns.

At the city’s commercial disposal price of $148 per tonne, diverting 1,500 tonnes would avoid $222,000 in disposal costs. Not all of that saving would accrue to the municipal budget because businesses currently pay haulers, but lower commercial costs strengthen the local economy and can be treated as a city benefit.

Using 0.42 kilograms as one meal, 1,500 tonnes represents 3.57 million meals. At the Social Services Department’s standard meal allowance of $7.20, the food has a value of $25.7 million. This comparison demonstrates that the program pays for itself many times over. It also excludes the value of avoided emissions, cleaner commercial bins, and reduced pressure on emergency food providers.

The same food might not have sold at full price, and a mixed locker is not identical to a purchased meal. Nevertheless, the meal allowance is the best available common unit. Applying a large discount would not change the conclusion; even at ten cents on the dollar, the food value would exceed total first-year cost by more than eight times.

## Relationship to food-waste prevention

Rescuing surplus is not as beneficial as preventing it. Businesses should first improve forecasting, portioning, and stock rotation. ShelfRoute guidance would place this hierarchy on the first page and would provide a weekly surplus report to each donor.

The report would show kilograms donated by product type. A business with repeated bread surpluses could reduce its final bake, while a supermarket with repeated salad donations could order fewer salads. This feedback is a genuine prevention function, not merely diversion.

There is a possibility that easy donation will make overproduction feel harmless. The city can address this by publishing a “steady donor” badge only for businesses whose donations decline over six months. A declining amount would be treated as evidence of improved forecasting. Businesses with rising donations would not lose access to collections, since excluding them would cause more disposal.

This measurement approach cannot distinguish prevention from falling sales, but either outcome means less surplus is entering the network. The city’s immediate logistics need is the same.

## Governance and responsibilities

The Library Service would own the crates, lockers, and transport process. The Office of Circular Services would recruit businesses, maintain guidance, and publish monthly results. The Department of Community Support would promote lockers to residents and community organizations.

Donors would retain responsibility for deciding that food is suitable when packed. The city would assume responsibility only for moving the sealed crate to its listed destination. Once a locker code is sent, responsibility would transfer to the recipient. These handoffs should limit confusion about ownership.

A ShelfRoute steering group would meet monthly. It would include the three departments, one library driver, two participating businesses, and one locker user. Meetings should focus on route changes rather than broad strategy. Major policy questions can be resolved by the City Manager because the network uses existing municipal assets.

The portal would record donor, weight, category, branch, van, locker, and collection time. Weight would usually be entered by the business rather than confirmed by a city scale. Purchasing scales for every branch is unnecessary when businesses already use kitchen or shipping scales. If no scale is available, the portal would assign the average weight for that crate color.

## Implementation schedule

Cabinet approval in July would permit procurement in August and installation in September.

- **August:** Order crates and lockers; modify van loading diagrams; recruit 150 initial businesses.
- **September:** Train branch staff and drivers; begin yellow and green crate movements across all six loops.
- **October:** Open public reservations at six locker sites; add blue crates on Harbor Bend and South Pair.
- **November:** Open the remaining six locker sites; recruit up to 450 businesses.
- **December:** Adjust routes and publish the first performance report.
- **January to June:** Continue operations and expand blue-crate acceptance if claims remain high.
- **July:** Decide whether to add schools, office cafeterias, and market traders.

The first eight weeks would have operational stop rules. A route would temporarily suspend food carriage if leakage damages library material twice, if the route exceeds its shift by more than 30 minutes on three evenings, or if over half its food is unclaimed. The affected route would resume after revised packing or locker arrangements are agreed. Other routes would continue.

Success at twelve months would mean recovery of 1,500 tonnes, participation by 450 businesses, an average locker claim rate of 60 percent, and no more than ten damaged books attributable to food transport. A lower tonnage should not by itself end the program if user demand is high, because meal value may remain substantial.

## Principal risks

### Food condition

The city cannot control every item packed by a donor. Labels, sealed crates, category exclusions, and short van journeys provide a practical level of control. The program should emphasize that recipients inspect items before use, just as they would inspect groceries at home.

Temperature is the main uncertainty for blue crates. Mechanical refrigeration would remove the cost advantage, so the city should rely on insulated covers, evening collection, and air-conditioned locker vestibules. Belden Quay has only about 30 evenings each year above 18 degrees Celsius. On those evenings, blue-crate service could continue if the donor labels the item for collection within two hours. The two-hour period would start when the item is entered into the portal because that is the first verifiable time.

### Disruption to library work

Food may leak, smell, or attract pests. Lidded crates and daily removal should make this uncommon. The stop rules protect any route experiencing repeated incidents. Cleaning costs are included, although the estimate assumes no major pest-control work.

Staff may object that the program adds duties without adding positions. Management should explain that ShelfRoute uses short periods of unused route and branch capacity. If every participating business delivered a crate daily, some large branches could receive 30 or more crates, but such consistent participation is unlikely at launch.

### Uneven access

Branches are not evenly distributed, and businesses in the western industrial strip are more than 800 metres from a library. The initial network would therefore favor central neighborhoods. This is acceptable because food waste is mobile and residents can collect from any locker. Once the network proves itself, the city could designate fire stations or recreation centers as satellite drop points.

Phone registration could exclude residents without reliable mobile service. Branch staff could issue a printed code on request. The portal should not require an address or proof of income.

### Weak demand or excessive demand

If food goes unclaimed, the city can consolidate listings into fewer lockers. If demand exceeds supply, the two-locker weekly limit distributes access. Because no income test applies, some food will go to residents who could afford it. That is not a loss: the food is still displaced from disposal, and universal access reduces administrative cost.

### Dependence on voluntary donors

The 450-business assumption is ambitious. Recruitment would begin with premises within 800 metres of a branch and would emphasize reduced bin volume and public recognition. If participation remains low, the city could require large premises to use ShelfRoute before renewing commercial organics exemptions. The legal basis for linking these matters has not been reviewed, but the possibility may encourage voluntary enrollment.

## Recommendation

Approve $311,000 and authorize the Library Service to launch ShelfRoute across all six transfer loops. Direct the Office of Circular Services to recruit 450 businesses, install twelve locker banks, and report monthly on donated weight, claims, route delays, and damage.

ShelfRoute makes use of capacity the city has already purchased. Its core transaction is simple: a shop fills a crate, a library van carries it on a journey already scheduled, and a resident collects it from a familiar public building. Even allowing for imperfect participation and unclaimed food, the scale of estimated surplus makes citywide implementation preferable to waiting for a separate food-rescue fleet.

# The Price of an Anvil

By the time Nara Senn reached Morrow’s Anvil, the asteroid had already bankrupted three kinds of people.

First came the investors, who had believed the assay drones. Then the freight companies, which had built tugs for cargoes that never moved. Last came the miners, who had accepted half their wages in company notes because there was nowhere to spend money inside a stone.

Now the creditors had sent Nara to put a price on what remained.

The shuttle matched rotation with the docking spindle. Beyond the porthole, Morrow’s Anvil turned against the stars: an iron-black potato girdled by silver radiator fins. Its mass driver ran along the equator like a pale scar. According to the prospectus, sixty-two million tonnes of nickel-iron waited inside, plus cobalt, platinum-group traces and enough silicate to shield every planned habitat between Earth and the Moon.

According to the market, it was worth less each morning.

Nara touched the nickel coin in her pocket. Her father had pressed it into her hand when the Belisar furnaces closed.

“First metal I ever poured,” he had said. “Keep it until metal matters again.”

That had been fourteen years earlier, on the day Morrow Extraction announced its discovery.

The announcement alone had lowered long-dated nickel contracts by eleven percent. No asteroid metal had reached Earth. No refinery had been built. Yet the possibility of cheap future supply had made two terrestrial mines unfinanceable, including Belisar. By the time engineers admitted that bringing Anvil’s metal down a gravity well would consume most of its value, her father’s furnace had been cut apart and sold.

A light blinked green over the shuttle hatch.

“Welcome, Appraiser Senn,” said a man waiting on the other side. He was tall, grey-bearded and held to the deck by magnetic sandals. “Lio Marr. Custodian, mechanic and, under Section Eight of the salvage code, continuous human possessor.”

“You’re maintaining the company’s lien by staying aboard?”

“Someone has to keep the lights on. The law merely makes my stubbornness useful.”

Behind him, the reception tunnel was lined with brass plaques bearing the names of investment funds, engineering syndicates and municipalities that had bought Morrow bonds. Dust floated in the stale air. Someone had drawn a moustache on the founder’s portrait.

Nara opened her case and presented the court seal. “I have four days to inventory the assets and set a liquidation reserve.”

Lio looked past her at the shuttle. “Did you bring a large scale?”

“I brought market models.”

“Then yours will break before mine does.”

He led her inward.

## I

The refinery occupied a cavern five hundred metres long. Under Nara’s lamp, crushers and induction furnaces emerged from the dark in sections, each one cleaner than she expected.

“Idle for nineteen months,” Lio said. “We cycle the bearings every sixth day. Furnace Three has a cracked bus plate. The volatile separator was never commissioned.”

“Why not?”

“No customers for volatiles. Everyone wanted metal then.”

He kicked off toward a rack of sample cylinders. Nara followed less gracefully, catching handrails whenever her case swung ahead of her.

The cylinders confirmed what the files had said. The ore was mostly iron and nickel, good enough for beams, tanks and radiation shielding. Platinum occurred in concentrations too small to justify separating unless the bulk metal already had a buyer. There was no hidden jewel inside the Anvil, only an extraordinary quantity of an ordinary thing.

At spot prices on Earth, the contained metal appeared to be worth a fortune. Subtract refining losses, transport, insurance, atmospheric entry and the cost of releasing millions of tonnes without crushing the market, and the fortune became a question mark.

“Founder Vey sold this as a mountain of coins,” Nara said.

“Pell Vey sold everything as something else. Ore became coins. Debt became growth. Delay became optionality.”

“You disliked him?”

“I stayed when he left.”

Pell Vey had died six months after the insolvency, when a private sailcraft failed to open its reflector. The estate claimed accident. The creditors’ committee called it irrelevant.

The ten-millionth tonne, arriving into a glutted market decades later, might be worth less than the energy required to heat it.

In her cabin, Nara opened the corporate charter. Extraction licenses could be severed from title. The mass driver’s metering system could authenticate annual quotas. The court order permitted her to divide movable assets into lots, though nobody seemed to have imagined dividing an ore body by calendar.

She worked until the air system dimmed the lights for night.

Instead of one asteroid, she constructed twenty-four time-limited rights.

The first lot included the existing inventory. The next five granted annual extraction quotas large enough to support Loom’s habitats. Later lots grew gradually, allowing buyers to reserve supply or suppress it, but only for a fixed year. Unused quotas would expire back to a custodial trust. A maintenance levy attached to every lot would keep the refinery operational. The machinery itself would remain with the trust until the final extraction right ended.

She ran the model. The present value exceeded the expected single-lot sale by nine percent, provided at least one terrestrial combine bid to preserve prices and at least one orbital builder bid for actual metal.

It depended on competitors wanting opposite things.

Most markets did.

At three in the morning, Lio found her in the galley.

“You have divided my rock into years,” he said, reading over her shoulder.

“The rock was always years. Vey disguised it as tonnes.”

“What happens after Year Twenty-Four?”

“The trust auctions a new schedule.”

“And if the machinery fails in Year Seven?”

“The levy covers expected maintenance.”

“Expected machinery is easy to maintain.”

She rubbed her eyes. “Do you have a better structure?”

“No. I have a list of pumps your model has not met.”

He sat opposite her. For a while the only sound was the recycler ticking in the wall.

“My father worked at Belisar,” Nara said.

Lio’s face changed, though not enough to call it pity.

“Then you know what this place did before we mined a gram.”

“I know what people said it did.”

“Same thing, in markets.”

She placed the nickel coin on the table. Its edge was worn smooth.

“Edda Rune says withholding Anvil protects towns like Belisar.”

“Possibly.”

“Pavi says releasing it builds new towns.”

“Possibly.”

“That word does too much work.”

“It gets paid less than certainty.” Lio slid the coin back to her. “Put it in your auction if you want an honest reserve. One old furnace, one failed asteroid and whatever your father thought metal was worth.”

## IV

The creditors objected immediately.

During the emergency hearing, their counsel called Nara’s plan untested, complicated and vulnerable to operational risk. The senior bond trustee wanted a clean sale and a payment before the quarter closed. The employee representative wanted unpaid wages placed ahead of maintenance. Lantern Recovery’s lawyers argued that annual rights would deprive title of its economic substance.

Pavi’s cooperative supported the plan, which made the trustee distrust it more.

Nara answered for two hours. A whole-asset bidder would discount the Anvil for market saturation, she explained. Separate annual quotas allowed each bidder to value only the period relevant to its business. Habitat builders could buy near-term supply without financing millions of unwanted tonnes. Terrestrial producers could bid for later years if orderly release genuinely had value. Competition between consumption and withholding would reveal a price that neither side alone would offer.

The judge approved the structure on the condition that Nara raise enough in the first six lots to cover priority claims and three years of maintenance.

“That condition can’t be met,” the bond trustee told her after the hearing.

“Then you’ll get your clean sale next week.”

“And your experiment will have lowered confidence in it.”

“Confidence is what financed this place.”

He did not answer.

The auction began at noon ship-time.

Nara sat in the old driver control room, facing a wall of inactive coil indicators. Lio watched from the doorway. Pavi participated from Loom’s rented berth. Edda Rune appeared as Lantern’s authorised representative, still wearing white.

Lot One contained the existing forty thousand tonnes.

Loom opened below reserve. A lunar breaker yard countered. Loom raised twice and stopped. With twelve seconds remaining, Cinder Bank confirmed its construction facility, and Pavi bid again.

Sold.

Pavi’s image froze with her mouth open, as if surprise were another form of signal delay.

Lots Two and Three sold to Loom after narrower contests. The prices were high enough to cover extraction but low enough to make the habitats feasible. Lot Four went to the breaker yard. Lot Five received no bids until Lantern entered at the reserve and acquired the entire quota.

“Why would they buy Year Five?” Lio asked.

“To remove it,” Nara said.

“They paid for nothing.”

“They paid for everybody else to have less.”

By Lot Six, the priority threshold was still short by sixteen million crowns.

The trustee sent Nara a message consisting only of the number.

Lot Six opened. Loom had reached its credit limit. The breaker yard bid once, then withdrew. Lantern offered eighty percent of reserve.

Nara watched the clock fall through thirty seconds.

If the lot failed, the judge’s condition failed with it. The auction would unwind. Lantern would likely purchase the whole Anvil the following week, cheaper than it could buy enough individual quotas to control production.

At twelve seconds, a new bidder registered: Danton Vale Metals Pension Fund.

Nara recognised the name as one of the employee funds that had lost value after Morrow’s discovery. It bid at reserve.

Lantern countered.

The pension fund bid again.

For ninety seconds the price climbed. Edda’s expression barely moved, but each Lantern bid came faster. The pension fund finally stopped at one hundred and forty-one percent of reserve.

Lantern took Lot Six.

The threshold indicator turned green.

Later lots produced stranger alliances. Loom bought Year Seven jointly with a freight guild. Lantern purchased Years Eight through Eleven. The pension fund acquired Year Twelve, apparently betting that it could resell the quota when terrestrial mines began to decline. A manufacturer of magnetic bearings bought only the cobalt by-product from Years Thirteen and Fourteen. Several distant lots went unsold.

At the end, projected creditor recovery stood at sixty-four cents on the crown. Employee wage claims would be paid in full. The maintenance trust had eight years of funding, assuming Lio’s pumps behaved like Nara’s expected machinery.

The bond trustee shook her hand without warmth.

Edda remained on the channel after the others left.

“You have made supply less predictable,” she said.

“I have made ownership less concentrated.”

“Lantern controls five of the next eleven years.”

“Not the first four.”

“We will let our quotas expire if conditions require it.”

“That is your right.”

“You understand that no metal will be produced in those years?”

“I understand you paid the creditors for the choice.”

Edda studied her across the delay. “You could work for us. We need people who understand that absence has a price.”

Nara ended the call.

## V

Three days later, the first bundle of Loom ingots entered the mass driver.

The launch was ceremonial only in the sense that Lio had cleaned the control room and Pavi had brought a bottle of something labelled wine. Nara suspected it had never encountered a grape.

The driver charged. A low vibration passed through the asteroid, more felt in the teeth than heard. On the display, the parcel accelerated down the equatorial track and vanished onto its transfer course.

Forty thousand tonnes would leave over the next year. After that, the refinery would process fresh ore for Lots Two and Three. In Year Five, if Lantern kept its promise to itself, the furnaces would cool again.

Pavi squeezed droplets of wine into three bulbs.

“To cheap metal,” she said.

“To adequately priced metal,” Nara replied.

Lio raised his bulb. “To pumps outside expected failure.”

They drank.

Through the observation port, the launched parcel was already invisible. Nara pictured it moving toward Loom’s unfinished habitat, where welders would turn an ingot into a curved wall, and a bank would call that wall collateral. She also pictured Belisar’s dismantled furnaces and the towns Edda had named, each depending on metal remaining expensive enough to dig from deep ground.

Her auction had not solved that contest. It had numbered the years in which each side might win.

Before departing, Nara visited the sample rack and asked Lio for a sliver from the first Anvil ingot. He cut one no larger than a fingernail. It was dull, granular and lighter in her palm than her father’s coin.

“You know they are nearly the same alloy,” Lio said.

“Not the same price.”

“Nothing has the same price in two places.”

At the shuttle hatch, Nara held both pieces of nickel together. One had come up from beneath Belisar in the last prosperous year. The other had crossed no distance at all and had still managed to close Belisar’s furnaces.

She left the old coin with Lio as a maintenance-trust asset, entered on the inventory at one crown.

The asteroid sliver she kept.

As the shuttle pulled away, Morrow’s Anvil diminished against the dark. Its mass driver flashed again, sending another bundle toward people who could use it. The asteroid was no smaller to the eye. At the current release rate, it would not look changed in Nara’s lifetime.

For the first time, she understood that abundance was not the opposite of scarcity. Abundance was scarcity waiting for a schedule.

# The Laboratory That Waits: Temporal Slack in Automated Experimental Workflows

## Abstract

Laboratory automation is usually evaluated through throughput, precision, and the proportion of operations performed without human intervention. Less attention is paid to waiting: idle robot arms, queued plates, stabilization periods, delayed human approvals, and instruments reserved for work that has not yet arrived. This review examines waiting as a feature of automated laboratories rather than simply as unused capacity. The literature can be divided into four broad accounts of waiting: waste to be removed, scientifically required dwell time, protective slack, and evidence of poor organizational coordination. Across these accounts, authors disagree about whether high equipment utilization indicates successful automation. Scheduling studies generally seek to compress idle periods, whereas reliability studies suggest that spare capacity can contain failures. Human-factors research adds that some machine waiting merely transfers urgency to technicians. The review argues that temporal slack should be measured separately from accidental delay, although the available literature rarely makes that distinction consistently. A provisional taxonomy is offered, followed by recommendations for designing automated workflows with visible queues, bounded recovery time, and limited spare capacity. The evidence remains fragmented, particularly for long-running biology workflows, but it indicates that the fastest automated laboratory is not necessarily the most productive or dependable one.

## 1. Introduction

The familiar image of laboratory automation is continuous motion. Plates travel between readers and incubators, liquid handlers dispense without interruption, and scheduling software fills every opening in an instrument calendar. Vendors and laboratory managers often describe this condition using the language of utilization: an expensive device creates value when it is operating and loses value when it is idle. This reasoning has encouraged laboratories to treat waiting as a defect.

Yet automated laboratories wait constantly. A sample may need thirty minutes for a reaction to develop. A robotic gripper may be held outside an enclosure while a centrifuge completes its cycle. A batch may remain in a queue because a scientist has not approved an anomalous control result. Instruments are also left deliberately unbooked so that failed runs can be repeated. These pauses are not equivalent, even though a scheduling dashboard may display each of them as an unproductive block of time.

The distinction matters because removing one kind of waiting can create another. If plates are released toward an analyzer as soon as preparation ends, they may accumulate in an uncontrolled queue beside the analyzer. If every incubator is kept full, a delayed plate may have nowhere to go. If software automatically proceeds through every decision point, scientists may discover a systematic problem only after large amounts of reagent and material have been consumed. Faster local operation can therefore produce slower or less reliable laboratory performance.

This review considers the role of temporal slack in automated experimental workflows. Temporal slack is defined here as time or capacity not assigned to immediate productive motion. The definition includes empty scheduling intervals, planned buffers, scientific dwell periods, and some forms of operator delay. This breadth makes it possible to connect literatures that are usually discussed separately, although it also risks treating unlike phenomena as parts of one category.

The central question is whether waiting should be minimized, tolerated, or designed. The literature does not provide one answer. Optimization research generally treats idle time as a cost, process-control research recognizes waiting as a physical constraint, and resilience research treats slack as an insurance mechanism. Human-factors studies further suggest that the distribution of waiting between machines and people affects fatigue and error. Bringing these positions together exposes a basic tension: laboratories want automated systems that are both highly occupied and immediately available when an exception occurs.

## 2. Scope of the Review

The review draws on publications concerning robotic laboratories, instrument scheduling, workflow orchestration, manufacturing cells, clinical sample processing, and human supervision of automation. Searches were conducted in several technical and scientific databases using combinations of terms such as “laboratory automation,” “idle time,” “scheduling,” “queue,” “incubation,” “workflow delay,” and “robot recovery.” References cited by relevant papers were also inspected. Studies were favored when they described a working system rather than only a scheduling algorithm, though several simulation papers were retained because little operational evidence was available.

Approximately two dozen sources formed the main body of the review. The literature was read narratively and grouped according to the function authors assigned to waiting. No formal quality score was applied because engineering case reports and observational laboratory studies were too different for a common scale. Manufacturing studies were included where the equipment arrangement resembled a laboratory workcell. Clinical laboratories were included selectively, particularly when they addressed sample queues or urgent insertions.

The resulting evidence base is uneven. Most reports concern short plate-based workflows or simulated jobs, while fewer examine experiments lasting days. Publications also tend to describe successful installations, and vendors rarely report how often automation is stopped, bypassed, or repaired. Nevertheless, the sources provide several recurring interpretations of temporal slack.

## 3. Waiting as Waste

The strongest tradition treats waiting as one of the principal losses that automation should remove. In this view, idle time indicates poor sequencing, inadequate equipment balancing, or failure to anticipate resource contention. Havel and Sorn’s simulation of the fictional Lattice-12 screening cell, for example, compared first-in-first-out scheduling with a priority rule based on predicted operation length. Their priority scheduler reduced average plate completion time by 17 percent, largely by preventing short jobs from becoming trapped behind long incubation-heavy jobs. The robot arm also spent less time waiting for destination instruments to become available.

Similar conclusions appear in reports on modular chemistry platforms. Neris and Volan described a synthesis system in which vessels repeatedly waited at a shared weighing station. Adding a second station raised daily output, but changing the order of weighing and solvent addition produced nearly the same gain without new hardware. The authors presented the queue as proof that the original workflow had been badly arranged.

These studies make an important contribution by showing that nominal instrument speed is not the same as system throughput. A pipetting device can operate faster while total run time remains unchanged because downstream readers or centrifuges determine the pace. Queue maps and event logs can reveal these constraints more reliably than raw utilization percentages. The literature also demonstrates that small scheduling choices may have larger effects than purchasing a faster robot.

However, the waste account tends to assume that every job has a stable duration and that the objective is known in advance. Real experiments often violate both assumptions. A liquid handler may pause because a tip cannot be detected, an imaging run may expand when additional fields are requested, and a control result may require interpretation. Optimization papers frequently model such events as random delays rather than scientifically meaningful decisions. Their solutions are therefore strongest for repetitive assays and less obviously applicable to research environments.

The emphasis on mean completion time can also obscure extreme cases. A rule that improves average throughput may leave a small number of temperature-sensitive samples waiting too long. In some studies, a reduction in robot idle time is reported as an improvement even when sample residence time is not measured. The literature thus occasionally treats machine motion as the product of the laboratory rather than validated experimental output.

## 4. Scientific Dwell Time

A second body of work concerns waiting that is required by the experiment. Incubation, settling, thermal equilibration, reaction development, instrument calibration, and washing all impose intervals during which visible progress may be limited. Such intervals are sometimes called “hard waits,” though the term is misleading because many are permitted ranges rather than exact durations.

Bellane’s review of automated immunoassay workcells distinguishes exact-time operations from minimum-time operations. An exact-time operation must occur near a specified moment, while a minimum-time operation may occur at any later time after a threshold. This distinction has scheduling consequences. A plate requiring at least twenty minutes of incubation can remain in place for twenty-five minutes if the assay tolerates it, whereas a plate that must be read within a two-minute window cannot safely join an ordinary queue.

Laboratory schedulers often represent both conditions as fixed durations. This simplifies software but may waste flexibility. In the Orison Enzyme Laboratory case described by Quill, expanding incubation requirements from single values to validated windows allowed the scheduler to interleave three assay families. Daily capacity reportedly increased from 38 to 51 plates without changes to the hardware. The result suggests that scientific protocols contain hidden temporal options that automation engineers can exploit.

At the same time, the literature sometimes implies that any protocol interval can be negotiated once enough data are collected. That is too broad. Some timing requirements arise from unstable chemistry, cell stress, or regulatory validation and cannot be altered merely because a scheduler would benefit. The Orison case involved relatively forgiving colorimetric assays, but it has been cited in discussions of cell culture and analytical chemistry where timing risks are different. Generalizing from it may encourage laboratories to widen windows without sufficient scientific validation.

There is also disagreement about whether scientific dwell time should count as equipment utilization. An incubator containing plates is clearly performing a function despite having no moving parts. A robot arm waiting beside it is not. Some dashboards count both devices as occupied because they are reserved for the workflow; others count only active operations. This inconsistency makes comparisons between laboratories unreliable. A system claiming 90 percent utilization may be reporting reservation, physical activity, or successful sample processing.

The most useful contribution of this literature is the recognition that workflow timing has several dimensions: minimum duration, maximum duration, permissible interruption, and sensitivity to variation. Yet few studies record all four. A basic operation is usually stored as a single number, leaving the scheduler unable to distinguish a harmless five-minute delay from one that invalidates a sample.

## 5. Slack as Protection Against Failure

Reliability studies reverse the usual interpretation of idle capacity. Instead of asking how to keep every instrument busy, they ask what happens when a busy instrument fails. A tightly scheduled laboratory may have no location for interrupted work, no opportunity to repeat a control, and no alternative path around an unavailable device. Under these conditions, high utilization can make a local fault propagate across the workcell.

Daro and Melsin examined fault logs from the invented MorrowBench facility, where six automated stations shared two transport robots. They found that stoppages lasting less than eight minutes caused most of the lost shift time. The delay came not from the original fault but from clearing plates that had continued arriving during recovery. Their proposed policy inserted ten-minute empty blocks every two hours. Simulations suggested lower nominal throughput but higher completed throughput once faults were included.

This finding aligns with research on manufacturing buffers, where small reserves can separate one machine’s variability from another. The analogy is appealing: a plate hotel resembles an intermediate storage buffer, and duplicate readers resemble redundant production machines. However, biological samples are not inert components. A plate hotel may protect the schedule while exposing cells or reagents to unacceptable temperature, humidity, or evaporation. Buffer capacity is therefore not automatically useful capacity.

Several authors recommend “recovery slack,” meaning time and space reserved for predictable categories of exception. Examples include an empty incubator position, an unassigned robot slot, spare consumables, and a scheduled period for reruns. This is more specific than simply lowering utilization. Recovery slack is linked to an action: holding a delayed sample, replacing a failed batch, or allowing an operator to inspect a deck.

Evidence for the ideal amount of slack is weak. MorrowBench’s ten-minute blocks were chosen from its local fault pattern, while other papers propose reserves of 5 to 20 percent with limited justification. The literature frequently repeats the idea that systems should run at about 80 percent utilization, apparently because queues rise rapidly near full capacity. That principle is plausible but not universal. A rarely failing reader with a large downstream buffer may safely operate near full occupancy, whereas a fragile transport robot could destabilize the laboratory at a much lower figure.

Some reliability papers also count unused duplicate equipment as slack even where the duplicate is required for routine throughput. This inflates the appearance of resilience. True redundancy exists only if an alternative resource remains available when the primary resource fails. Two instruments that are both continuously booked do not provide much practical redundancy, even if either can technically perform the same assay.

## 6. Human Waiting and Transferred Urgency

Automated workflows include human decisions at loading, approval, replenishment, exception handling, and data review. Waiting can therefore be shifted rather than eliminated. A machine may operate continuously because a technician is expected to respond immediately whenever a consumable runs low. Conversely, a machine may remain idle because approvals are performed in scheduled batches.

In a study of the fictional North Aster Sample Centre, Pellen and Uro observed technicians supervising three automated preparation lines. The lines generated frequent low-priority notices mixed with occasional urgent alarms. Technicians responded quickly to almost all alerts because the interface did not clearly show whether a delay would damage a sample. As a result, staff repeatedly abandoned manual tasks to check machines that could have waited. The automation reduced direct pipetting but increased fragmented attention.

This work provides a useful correction to equipment-centered studies. A scheduler that reduces robot waiting by demanding instant human intervention may improve its own performance while worsening laboratory performance. Interruptions can increase setup errors, delay documentation, and make work harder to plan. The relevant question is not simply whether the robot waits, but who waits, under what pressure, and with what consequence.

Human-factors authors commonly recommend escalation windows. Instead of issuing an immediate alarm, the system should state that a response is required within a defined period, such as “refill tips within 18 minutes.” This converts an interruption into a schedulable task. Some interfaces also group non-urgent interventions into service rounds. These approaches appear sensible, although evidence is mainly observational and based on staff preference rather than measured error rates.

The literature occasionally assumes that human waiting is inherently more costly than machine waiting because labor is flexible and expensive. This is not always true. A specialist may use a waiting period to review data or prepare another protocol, whereas an idle dedicated analyzer may have no alternate use. Cost depends on whether waiting prevents other productive activity, not merely on whether a person or device is stationary.

There is also a risk of romanticizing human judgment. Several case reports describe operators as a flexible buffer who can rescue irregular workflows. In practice, this may mean that incomplete automation is sustained through unrecorded manual work. If technicians regularly rearrange queues, carry plates past a failed transporter, or reinterpret ambiguous alerts, the system may appear more autonomous and robust than it is. Waiting records should therefore include human interventions, but most automation logs track only machine states.

## 7. Organizational Waiting

A final category lies outside the physical workcell. Automated runs wait for protocol approval, reagent release, sample registration, data transfer, or access to shared instruments. These delays can exceed the time saved by faster liquid handling, yet they receive less attention because they belong to different software and management systems.

Sivert’s study of the Veyra Materials Unit found that a robot completed formulation batches in four hours, but batches spent a median of nineteen hours awaiting analytical review. The unit initially planned to buy a second formulation robot. After mapping the end-to-end process, it introduced two review periods per day and standardized the data packet sent to analysts. Turnaround reportedly fell more than it would have under the equipment expansion scenario.

This case illustrates the value of measuring the entire workflow. Automation can accelerate one stage while leaving the governing bottleneck elsewhere. It also shows why utilization is an incomplete management measure: the formulation robot was busy, but completed knowledge moved slowly.

Nonetheless, organizational waiting is only loosely connected to the scheduling literature reviewed above. A delay caused by an approval meeting differs from a plate waiting for an available reader. The remedies involve staffing, authority, and information design rather than robotic coordination. Combining them under temporal slack may create a broad vocabulary at the expense of causal precision.

Several publications propose digital integration as the general solution. If the laboratory information system, scheduler, and analysis pipeline exchange status automatically, approvals can supposedly occur earlier and queues become visible. Integration may help, but visibility does not itself add reviewing capacity or resolve unclear responsibility. The literature often overstates what software connectivity can accomplish in organizations where decisions remain contested or under-resourced.

## 8. Toward a Taxonomy of Laboratory Waiting

The reviewed literature supports a provisional classification with five categories:

1. **Constraint waiting** arises from scientific or physical requirements, such as incubation or thermal equilibration.
2. **Contention waiting** occurs when multiple jobs need the same robot, instrument, or storage position.
3. **Recovery waiting** is time reserved or consumed while faults are diagnosed and work is restored.
4. **Decision waiting** occurs when a human or analytical system must authorize the next operation.
5. **Administrative waiting** reflects registration, release, documentation, or organizational coordination.

This taxonomy is useful because the categories suggest different responses. Constraint waiting should be scientifically characterized, contention waiting may be reduced by scheduling, recovery waiting requires fault planning, decision waiting benefits from explicit response windows, and administrative waiting may require process redesign.

However, the categories overlap. A plate awaiting review might occupy an incubator and thereby cause contention. A scientific constraint may become administrative when a validated timing window cannot be changed without formal approval. Recovery from a fault may require a human decision. It is therefore difficult to assign every delay to a single class. A better logging system might record both the immediate state and the underlying cause, though no reviewed system did so comprehensively.

The taxonomy also does not settle which waits are beneficial. Constraint waiting is necessary but not necessarily slack, while recovery slack may remain unused for long periods. Administrative waiting is usually undesirable, yet a review pause may prevent continuation of a faulty experiment. The categories clarify mechanisms more than value.

## 9. Discussion

Three conclusions recur across the literature. First, equipment utilization should not be used alone to judge laboratory automation. It can reward systems that keep devices occupied while increasing queues, sample risk, or operator interruption. Measures such as valid outputs per day, time within protocol windows, recovery duration, and human intervention load provide a broader picture.

Second, waiting should be represented explicitly in workflow models. Protocols need more than a sequence of active steps. They should identify timing ranges, holding conditions, interruptibility, decision deadlines, and acceptable recovery paths. Without these properties, a scheduler cannot distinguish useful flexibility from dangerous delay.

Third, some spare capacity appears necessary for resilience. The literature supports reserving at least a modest amount of time or storage for reruns and disruptions. A general target of 10 to 20 percent unassigned capacity seems reasonable across many laboratories, especially where workflows are variable. This recommendation should be interpreted cautiously because the studies do not directly compare reserve levels across different laboratory types. Even so, operating every critical resource at maximum occupancy is unlikely to be safe.

These conclusions are limited by the evidence. Many studies are simulations, single-site reports, or descriptions written during system deployment. Few provide raw event logs, and definitions of idle time differ. Research laboratories, diagnostic facilities, and manufacturing cells are often discussed together despite having different objectives. The literature also contains little information about failed automation projects, making it difficult to estimate whether slack prevents failure or merely accompanies well-funded systems.

More empirical work should compare laboratories before and after changes to scheduling slack. Such studies should report completed valid experiments, sample losses, staff interruptions, energy use, and recovery time rather than only robot utilization. Long-running workflows deserve particular attention because a short interruption can interact with multi-day biological processes in ways not captured by plate-handling simulations.

Despite these gaps, managers can take several immediate steps. They can separate active processing from reservation in equipment dashboards, record why a sample is waiting, validate timing windows instead of using single durations, and identify where interrupted samples can be held. Alert interfaces should display response deadlines. Finally, capacity planning should include ordinary faults rather than calculating output from perfect cycle times.

## 10. Conclusion

Waiting in automated laboratories is neither a single form of waste nor an uncomplicated source of safety. Some waiting is imposed by science, some results from contention, some preserves room for recovery, and some reveals organizational delay. The literature is strongest when it maps queues and timing constraints at the level of the whole workflow. It is weakest when it assumes that greater motion means greater productivity or, conversely, that an arbitrary reserve guarantees resilience.

Laboratory automation should therefore be designed around controlled waiting. Pauses should have known causes, acceptable durations, and defined consequences. A laboratory that can explain why its machines are idle may be better automated than one in which every instrument is busy and no resource is available when the experiment departs from plan.
