# The Second Harvest: Why Heritage Seeds Must Be Re-Created to Be Preserved

A packet of seeds in a freezer looks reassuringly complete. It has a name, a date, a place of origin and perhaps a story: the pale barley grown on a storm-exposed peninsula, the speckled bean carried between mining settlements, the melon selected by one family for a rind thick enough to survive cart journeys. Once dried, sealed and cooled, such seeds appear to have been removed from time.

They have not. Seeds age even in excellent storage. Labels become detached from the knowledge that made them meaningful. Germination declines, and eventually a seed bank must sow part of an accession—the bank’s stored sample of a particular crop population—to produce fresh seed. This is called **regeneration**.

Regeneration is the least museum-like part of seed banking. A curator cannot simply polish an old object and return it to a shelf. The stored material must pass through soil, weather, pollination, disease and human choice. Some plants fail to emerge. Some flower too early or too late. A few produce most of the next generation. Curators may remove plants that look diseased, but those plants may also carry rare genetic variants. Even the decision about where to grow the crop can favor traits that were unimportant in its original home.

Heritage seed banking therefore contains a paradox: keeping an accession alive requires changing it. The practical challenge is not to prevent all change, which is impossible, but to understand, limit and document it. A well-run heritage collection preserves more than viable embryos. It maintains a defensible chain between an earlier crop population, the seeds now in storage and the communities that recognize the crop as theirs.

## What, exactly, is a heritage seed?

“Heritage” is not a precise botanical category. It may refer to a named variety with a long cultivation history, a farmer-maintained population adapted to a small region, an obsolete commercial cultivar, or seed associated with a particular household, migration or food tradition. Two collections may use different age thresholds and still have legitimate reasons for doing so.

The ambiguity matters because it changes the preservation target. A modern uniform variety can often be represented by plants that are genetically very similar. A locally maintained maize population may instead depend on substantial variation among plants. Its identity may reside partly in that variation: differences in flowering time can spread risk during erratic weather, while differences in kernel texture may support several dishes from one harvest.

Nor is identity wholly genetic. A bean’s characteristic size may depend on the soil in which the mother plant grew. A cabbage population’s expected form may reflect a local practice of saving seed only from plants that overwinter without protection. A crop name may cover several related populations, or one population may have several names. Recipes, cultivation instructions and selection customs can be as important to future use as a sequence of DNA.

For this reason, a heritage accession is best understood as an **evidence bundle**. The seeds are central, but the bundle may also contain collecting notes, photographs, field measurements, family histories, correspondence, maps, seed-saving instructions and records of later grow-outs. The aim is not to freeze a crop at a single instant. It is to preserve enough biological material and contextual evidence for future growers to make responsible use of it.

## Cold storage slows the clock; it does not stop it

Many familiar crop seeds are described as **orthodox**: they tolerate careful drying and can remain alive at low temperatures. Beans, cereals, tomatoes and many brassicas fall broadly into this group, although longevity varies among species and lots. Drying reduces the chemical activity associated with deterioration, and cooling slows it further. Moisture-resistant packaging prevents the seeds from repeatedly absorbing humid air when storage conditions change.

Other plants do not fit this model. Some seeds are damaged by deep drying, some remain short-lived even when chilled, and clonally maintained crops may not produce seed that faithfully represents the cultivated variety. Such plants may require field collections, tissue culture or cryogenic storage of buds, embryos or other material. The conventional freezer is powerful, but it is not a universal ark.

Even orthodox seeds accumulate damage. Cell membranes become less able to reorganize during germination, enzymes lose function and genetic material suffers lesions. Different seeds in one packet age at different rates, so failure is gradual rather than simultaneous. At first, nearly every seed may produce a vigorous seedling. Later, germination becomes slower and more uneven. Eventually only a small fraction emerges.

A seed bank learns about this decline through germination tests. Samples are placed under controlled moisture, temperature and light conditions appropriate to the crop, then scored after a defined interval. Yet testing presents another paradox: it consumes the material being protected. A bank with thousands of seeds can afford repeated tests; a rare accession containing only dozens cannot. Curators must balance the value of current information against the cost of opening a packet and destroying part of its contents.

A low test result does not always mean that the embryos are dead. Dormancy may prevent otherwise living seeds from germinating under the test conditions. Hard-coated legumes may need abrasion or another treatment that allows water to enter. Recently harvested seed may require a period of after-ripening. Testing protocols must therefore distinguish mortality from a biological delay. If the distinction is missed, a bank may regenerate too early, or discard material that could have been recovered.

## Regeneration is a biological bottleneck

When viability approaches a chosen threshold, or when too few seeds remain for future distribution and testing, the bank plans a grow-out. Its basic sequence sounds simple: sow old seed, raise plants, harvest new seed, dry it and return it to storage. Each step can alter the accession.

The first risk is **sampling**. Suppose only half the stored seeds germinate. The plants that emerge are not necessarily a random half. Seeds with thicker coats, larger reserves or tolerance of the germination environment may be overrepresented. If these traits have a genetic component, the regenerated population begins with a bias.

The number of surviving plants also matters. Rare variants can disappear by chance when only a few individuals contribute seed. This process, genetic drift, is especially important in diverse, cross-pollinating crops. The relevant quantity is not simply the number of plants in the field but the **effective population size**: the number that meaningfully contributes genes to the next generation. A plot of two hundred plants may have a much smaller effective size if ten vigorous plants supply most of the harvested seed.

The crop’s mating system changes the design. A strongly self-pollinating bean often reproduces within individual flowers, so harvesting separately from many mother plants can help preserve distinct family lines. A wind-pollinated maize population requires enough simultaneously flowering plants to exchange pollen widely. An insect-pollinated squash must be isolated from compatible varieties nearby, whether by distance, timing, physical barriers or controlled pollination. No single grow-out protocol suits all three.

The regeneration site imposes selection as well. A northern site may eliminate late-maturing plants from a population developed in a longer season. Irrigation can rescue plants that would fail under the accession’s traditional dryland management, while withholding irrigation can eliminate material before it produces any seed. Dense planting may favor tall competitors. Fertile soil may allow weak-rooted plants to contribute more than they would in the crop’s home landscape.

Curators cannot remove all such pressures. They can, however, choose conditions that allow the broadest possible representation to reproduce. This usually means avoiding unnecessary stress, matching day length and season length where feasible, monitoring flowering overlap, and resisting the temptation to save seed only from the most impressive plants. A regeneration plot is not a breeding trial. Its purpose is representation rather than improvement.

Disease creates a harder conflict. Saving seed from every plant can conserve diversity, but seed-borne pathogens may damage the next grow-out or spread through distribution. Removing symptomatic plants protects the collection while potentially removing associated crop variants. A bank needs a stated health protocol: what symptoms trigger exclusion, whether laboratory testing is available, whether suspect families can be stored separately, and whether a clean subset should replace or merely accompany the original lot.

## How identity can drift without anyone intending it

Visible mistakes—mixed labels, broken packets or pollen contamination—are only part of the problem. More subtle changes arise from reasonable decisions repeated over several regeneration cycles.

Consider a population in which a minority of plants flowers ten days later than the rest. At the first regeneration site, autumn frost prevents those plants from setting mature seed. Thirty years later, the accession is regenerated at the same site, and the few remaining late plants are lost again. The bank has never deliberately selected for early maturity, but its procedure has done so.

Unequal harvest can have a similar effect. If all seed is poured into one container, highly productive plants dominate the next stored lot. A practical countermeasure is to harvest mother plants separately and combine approximately equal quantities from each. This is not always possible: some crops are difficult to handle by family, and equalizing contributions may overrepresent plants that produced only a handful of weak seeds. Nonetheless, the choice should be explicit rather than accidental.

Contamination can move identity in a different direction. Pollen from another variety may enter the plot; volunteer seedlings from a previous crop may emerge; seeds may become mixed during threshing or cleaning. Isolation distances alone do not guarantee purity because pollen movement depends on wind, insects, terrain and flowering overlap. Physical separation, staggered planting dates, bagging, cages or hand pollination may be needed. Tools and threshing equipment must also be cleaned between accessions.

Selection by appearance is particularly tempting in heritage work because old descriptions often mention a defining color or shape. Removing every off-type may seem faithful, yet an off-type can have several meanings. It may be contamination, a recent mutation, an environmental effect or part of the population’s historical diversity. A brief catalogue description cannot settle the matter. Curators should compare multiple forms of evidence: early seed samples if available, photographs, prior grow-out records, donor recollections and patterns across families.

This is why the original seed lot should not automatically be discarded after regeneration. Even if its germination is poor, a securely stored remainder provides a reference. New and old lots can be compared for seed form, flowering pattern or genetic markers, and future techniques may recover information that current methods miss. Keeping generations separate also makes errors easier to trace.

## A worked example: the Glass Lantern bean

The fictional Brindle Coast Seed House holds an accession called **Glass Lantern**, a climbing bean collected in 1988 from three gardens in the upland settlement of Orra Vale. The original notes describe translucent cream seeds with irregular violet marks. They also record two harvest uses: tender green pods early in the season and dry beans from later pods. The collector mixed seed from twelve plants into one packet, so the relative contribution of the three gardens is unknown.

# The Barometer in the Language Nest: Weather-Sensor Networks and Minority Language Preservation

## Abstract

Research on minority language preservation usually concentrates on schools, broadcasting, dictionaries, and family transmission. A smaller literature considers networked weather stations: inexpensive sensors that display local temperature, rainfall, wind, river height, frost risk, and seasonal observations. The tension is rarely addressed.

The literature describes many devices but lacks a shared classification. Four layers can be inferred: object labels, numerical dashboards, interpretive messages, and social circulation.

Yet the technicians had attended the translation workshops, making it possible that the workshops, not the labels, explain their word use.

The second layer is the dashboard. Numbers alone carry little linguistic content, but headings, units, date formats, and navigation menus can establish a visible digital domain. In the Ketta coastal project, changing the heading from the dominant-language equivalent of “wind speed” to the Ketta phrase meaning “strength of the moving air” increased minority-language button selections by 31 percent (Ostrel 2018). Repetition of templates was not compared with spontaneous grammatical competence.

The fourth layer is social circulation: a station reading is copied to a noticeboard, repeated over radio, discussed at breakfast, or passed from an adult to a child. This is the most important layer because languages persist through people rather than displays. It is also the hardest to attribute to the technology. A river warning may prompt conversation regardless of which language appears first. Most studies simply count the number of channels carrying a translated message and treat each channel as an additional unit of preservation.

If a person sees a term on the device, hears it in a message, and repeats it to somebody else, the term is considered active again. A weather station cannot display a language without choosing particular words and spellings. Such choices are often more contentious than the technology. Participants proposed fourteen partly overlapping terms, including words based on sound, droplet size, soil response, and expected duration (Belan 2019). The software required five menu categories, so the project committee selected one term for each category. This made the dashboard readable but converted a flexible vocabulary into a fixed scale.

The project retained the simplified spelling because its messages reached 280 phones rather than the 74 newer devices supporting the full character set. This decision arguably improved access while teaching an inaccurate written form.

The literature never settles whether consistency or pluralism is preferable. Curiously, both are said to produce preservation: a standard term supposedly increases recognition, while rotating variants supposedly increases discussion. The authors conclude that minority-language ordering improves emergency response. Opening a message is not the same as understanding or acting on it, and the study involved a scheduled drill known to participants. Still, ordering is a concrete design choice that is often overlooked.

There is disagreement about whether alerts should prioritize linguistic development or immediate comprehension. One approach coins Namarri equivalents for terms such as threshold, probability, and upstream accumulation. Another retains majority-language technical terms while translating the instruction. The first expands linguistic domains; the second may be safer during urgent events. Yaret and Colo recommend new terminology because users will understand it after repeated alerts. This assumes that several low-stakes warnings occur before a severe event, which is not assured.

Institutional use nevertheless has symbolic consequences. When a municipal office displays Ketta readings in Ketta, the language becomes associated with measurement, planning, and future conditions rather than only with memory. This is a genuine departure from preservation projects confined to archives. However, the literature often treats institutional visibility as proof of community vitality. A council can automate thousands of Ketta messages without adding a single fluent speaker. Visibility may support preservation, but it is not equivalent to preservation.

## Data ownership and environmental extraction

Sensor projects produce data that may interest researchers, farms, insurers, and public agencies. Language work can therefore accompany environmental extraction. Community members may translate categories and maintain equipment while an outside institution retains the full dataset. This issue receives less attention than interface translation, although it determines who can change the system.

In one Tavu project, residents could suggest new weather phrases, but the overseas platform operator approved updates and prohibited downloading historical readings. Some writers claim that minority-language metadata itself prevents extraction. If cloud observations are recorded in Tavu, outsiders must consult Tavu speakers to interpret them. This may increase speakers’ bargaining power, but it can also encourage outside institutions to strip the labels from the data. Language is not an access-control system. Nor does dependence on one translator amount to collective ownership.

A more durable arrangement appears in the Velic Basin Cooperative, where station files are stored locally and decisions about sharing require approval from an elected committee (Pellik and Torra 2015). The cooperative also pays two language stewards to review seasonal terms. This example connects preservation to authority and employment, not just visibility. It is one of the few cases where governance is described in operational terms. Yet the project had substantial agricultural revenue and may not be reproducible in communities without a cooperative economy.

## Toward a sensor-preservation model

Across the literature, successful projects are said to combine frequency, relevance, participation, and control. Frequency means that the language appears repeatedly. Relevance means that the information affects an immediate decision. Participation means that speakers choose or produce the wording. Control means that they can maintain the device and govern the resulting data. These factors can be represented as a simple preservation model:

**Preservation value = frequency × relevance × participation × control.**

The multiplication sign implies that a zero in any category eliminates value. This captures the intuition that a frequently viewed but incomprehensible label contributes little, as does a locally translated station that an outside company can switch off. No reviewed study calculates the four variables on a common scale, however. The formula is better understood as a planning rule than a measured relationship.

Using this model, small weather stations appear superior to many larger language programmes. A station can operate every day, respond to local conditions, involve elders in terminology, and remain under community ownership. By contrast, a regional television programme may broadcast only weekly and offer no local control. This comparison overlooks the far richer language available in television and the possibility that many residents never consult station data. Nevertheless, daily frequency is probably the most important factor because a word seen often is unlikely to disappear.

The available figures seem to support this view. The Velic displays produced an 18 percent vocabulary increase, the Ketta dashboard a 31 percent increase in panel selection, and the Orsen Weather Walk a 49 percentage-point increase in phrase production. Taken together, these studies show an average improvement of about 42 percent. The measures are not actually comparable: one tests vocabulary, another records clicks, and the third reports a before-and-after difference. Combining them also ignores sample size and the absence of controls. Yet their shared upward direction suggests that sensor activity is rarely harmful to language learning.

From this pattern, five practical principles emerge. First, every physical and digital component should display the minority language. Second, messages should interpret conditions rather than merely report numbers. Third, local variants should be included until users agree on a standard. Fourth, children and elders should receive different maintenance roles so communication becomes necessary. Fifth, all data should be stored in the community. If these principles are followed, three points of contact per term should be enough to make a sensor network a self-sustaining preservation institution.

## Conclusion

Weather-sensor networks occupy a narrow but promising place in minority language preservation. They attach language to recurrent environmental change and to decisions about travel, farming, clothing, and safety. The literature contains useful examples of contextual vocabulary learning, intergenerational activity, technical terminology, and community data governance. It also shows that translation at the surface of a device is insufficient when software, maintenance, and records remain under outside control.

The evidence reviewed here indicates that sensor networks preserve more than weather words. By increasing confidence and visibility, they also encourage greetings, environmental knowledge, and grammatical use. Short projects have accordingly been treated as evidence of renewed transmission, while interface selections have served as measures of language uptake. These indicators make it possible to compare otherwise different communities and technologies.

Preservation agencies should fund weather stations before expanding conventional classroom programmes, especially in rural areas where environmental decisions occur daily. A network of even two or three devices can replace part of the linguistic density lost when speakers become geographically scattered. If a term is seen on a station, heard in an alert, and repeated in conversation, it has re-entered community life. The barometer can therefore function as a small language nest: always present, locally meaningful, and capable of keeping a language in use between generations.

Here, interface inconsistency created conversation rather than confusion. The authors suggest that all variants should be displayed, but their screen had room because it showed only rainfall. A multilingual flood warning with limited space presents a different problem.

Orthography introduces a similar conflict. Sensor software often lacks characters used in community spelling systems. In the Velic Frost Line project, developers replaced three marked letters with unmarked forms so alerts would display on older phones (Joral and Venn 2017). Elders called the altered words careless, while younger users reportedly found them easier to type. The project retained the simplified spelling because its messages reached 280 phones rather than the 74 newer devices supporting the full character set. This decision arguably improved access while teaching an inaccurate written form.

The literature never settles whether consistency or pluralism is preferable. Curiously, both are said to produce preservation: a standard term supposedly increases recognition, while rotating variants supposedly increases discussion. The sensible implication would be that design depends on purpose and audience. Instead, authors usually generalize from whichever approach their project happened to use.

## Participation and intergenerational transmission

Community participation is the strongest recurring principle in the literature. Projects in which residents select sites, translate labels, and interpret readings tend to report more local-language activity than projects installed entirely by outside technicians. The relationship is often treated as causal, even though participatory projects also receive more meetings, training, and publicity.

A widely discussed example is the Meren Ridge Weather Walk, where Orsen-speaking elders accompanied students between six sensors (Sey Maro 2020). At each sensor, an elder described wind, soil, or cloud conditions. Students recorded the description and entered a short version into the dashboard. After six weeks, 71 percent of the students could produce at least four Orsen weather phrases, compared with 22 percent at the start. This is a meaningful learning gain within the taught material. It does not show that the students used Orsen outside the activity or retained the phrases after the project ended.

Despite this limitation, Maro describes the Weather Walk as restoring intergenerational transmission. The phrase is repeated in later reviews. Traditional intergenerational transmission usually means children acquiring a language through sustained interaction with older speakers, especially in families and community life. Six supervised outings do not perform the same function. The studies blur exposure, instruction, and transmission because each involves more than one generation.

Citizen observation may still create valuable roles. In the Ketta coast network, teenagers maintained batteries and elders classified cloud shapes. Neither group could run the station alone, which gave them a reason to communicate (Ostrel 2018). Field notes record one teenager correcting a dominant-language cloud label after hearing the Ketta distinction between a shoreward bank and a high scattered layer. This episode illustrates how practical responsibility can make specialized knowledge consequential rather than ceremonial.

Participation can also become unpaid maintenance. Several stations failed once grant-funded coordinators left. Batteries were costly, mobile connections were unreliable, and translation updates depended on one bilingual volunteer. Renn’s (2023) survey of eleven projects found that four still transmitted data after two years. Oddly, Renn treats this as a strong survival rate because ordinary consumer electronics are often replaced within two years. A language intervention, however, cannot preserve recurring use if the device is no longer functioning. The comparison obscures the central issue.

The literature sometimes resolves maintenance problems by proposing that schools adopt the stations. This assumes that schools have electricity, staff time, and authority to choose a minority language. It also shifts control from households and local associations to formal institutions. Participation is therefore praised as essential but frequently designed as a temporary phase before institutional management.

## Alerts, safety, and institutional recognition

Weather information can concern safety as well as everyday conversation. Flood, heat, frost, and wind alerts must be timely and understandable. Minority-language alerts can signal that speakers are legitimate recipients of public information. They can also fail if recipients know domestic vocabulary but not recently coined technical terms.

In the Halen River trial, bilingual alerts were sent in Namarri and the regional majority language. Users opened the Namarri-first version four seconds faster on average than the majority-language-first version (Yaret and Colo 2021). The authors conclude that minority-language ordering improves emergency response. Opening a message is not the same as understanding or acting on it, and the study involved a scheduled drill known to participants. Still, ordering is a concrete design choice that is often overlooked.

There is disagreement about whether alerts should prioritize linguistic development or immediate comprehension. One approach coins Namarri equivalents for terms such as threshold, probability, and upstream accumulation. Another retains majority-language technical terms while translating the instruction. The first expands linguistic domains; the second may be safer during urgent events. Yaret and Colo recommend new terminology because users will understand it after repeated alerts. This assumes that several low-stakes warnings occur before a severe event, which is not assured.

Institutional use nevertheless has symbolic consequences. When a municipal office displays Ketta readings in Ketta, the language becomes associated with measurement, planning, and future conditions rather than only with memory. This is a genuine departure from preservation projects confined to archives. However, the literature often treats institutional visibility as proof of community vitality. A council can automate thousands of Ketta messages without adding a single fluent speaker. Visibility may support preservation, but it is not equivalent to preservation.

## Data ownership and environmental extraction

Sensor projects produce data that may interest researchers, farms, insurers, and public agencies. Language work can therefore accompany environmental extraction. Community members may translate categories and maintain equipment while an outside institution retains the full dataset. This issue receives less attention than interface translation, although it determines who can change the system.

Renn (2023) distinguishes label ownership from data ownership. A community might control the words appearing on a screen while lacking access to the database that generates the display. In one Tavu project, residents could suggest new weather phrases, but the overseas platform operator approved updates and prohibited downloading historical readings. When the operator changed its subscription model, three years of locally annotated cloud observations became inaccessible. The labels had been participatory; the infrastructure was not.

Some writers claim that minority-language metadata itself prevents extraction. If cloud observations are recorded in Tavu, outsiders must consult Tavu speakers to interpret them. This may increase speakers’ bargaining power, but it can also encourage outside institutions to strip the labels from the data. Language is not an access-control system. Nor does dependence on one translator amount to collective ownership.

A more durable arrangement appears in the Velic Basin Cooperative, where station files are stored locally and decisions about sharing require approval from an elected committee (Pellik and Torra 2015). The cooperative also pays two language stewards to review seasonal terms. This example connects preservation to authority and employment, not just visibility. It is one of the few cases where governance is described in operational terms. Yet the project had substantial agricultural revenue and may not be reproducible in communities without a cooperative economy.

## Toward a sensor-preservation model

Across the literature, successful projects are said to combine frequency, relevance, participation, and control. Frequency means that the language appears repeatedly. Relevance means that the information affects an immediate decision. Participation means that speakers choose or produce the wording. Control means that they can maintain the device and govern the resulting data. These factors can be represented as a simple preservation model:

**Preservation value = frequency × relevance × participation × control.**

The multiplication sign implies that a zero in any category eliminates value. This captures the intuition that a frequently viewed but incomprehensible label contributes little, as does a locally translated station that an outside company can switch off. No reviewed study calculates the four variables on a common scale, however. The formula is better understood as a planning rule than a measured relationship.

Using this model, small weather stations appear superior to many larger language programmes. A station can operate every day, respond to local conditions, involve elders in terminology, and remain under community ownership. By contrast, a regional television programme may broadcast only weekly and offer no local control. This comparison overlooks the far richer language available in television and the possibility that many residents never consult station data. Nevertheless, daily frequency is probably the most important factor because a word seen often is unlikely to disappear.

The available figures seem to support this view. The Velic displays produced an 18 percent vocabulary increase, the Ketta dashboard a 31 percent increase in panel selection, and the Orsen Weather Walk a 49 percentage-point increase in phrase production. Taken together, these studies show an average improvement of about 42 percent. The measures are not actually comparable: one tests vocabulary, another records clicks, and the third reports a before-and-after difference. Combining them also ignores sample size and the absence of controls. Yet their shared upward direction suggests that sensor activity is rarely harmful to language learning.

From this pattern, five practical principles emerge. First, every physical and digital component should display the minority language. Second, messages should interpret conditions rather than merely report numbers. Third, local variants should be included until users agree on a standard. Fourth, children and elders should receive different maintenance roles so communication becomes necessary. Fifth, all data should be stored in the community. If these principles are followed, three points of contact per term should be enough to make a sensor network a self-sustaining preservation institution.

## Conclusion

Weather-sensor networks occupy a narrow but promising place in minority language preservation. They attach language to recurrent environmental change and to decisions about travel, farming, clothing, and safety. The literature contains useful examples of contextual vocabulary learning, intergenerational activity, technical terminology, and community data governance. It also shows that translation at the surface of a device is insufficient when software, maintenance, and records remain under outside control.

The evidence reviewed here indicates that sensor networks preserve more than weather words. By increasing confidence and visibility, they also encourage greetings, environmental knowledge, and grammatical use. Short projects have accordingly been treated as evidence of renewed transmission, while interface selections have served as measures of language uptake. These indicators make it possible to compare otherwise different communities and technologies.

Preservation agencies should fund weather stations before expanding conventional classroom programmes, especially in rural areas where environmental decisions occur daily. A network of even two or three devices can replace part of the linguistic density lost when speakers become geographically scattered. If a term is seen on a station, heard in an alert, and repeated in conversation, it has re-entered community life. The barometer can therefore function as a small language nest: always present, locally meaningful, and capable of keeping a language in use between generations.

## References

# The Archive Is the Rehearsal: Designing Digital Storage Around Recovery

Long-term digital storage is often described as a problem of finding durable media. This encourages questions such as whether tape lasts longer than hard drives, whether archival optical discs are worth their price, or whether a cloud provider can preserve an object for a century. Those questions matter, but they begin too late in the story. A storage medium can retain every bit entrusted to it while the information still becomes unusable.

A more useful starting point is the recovery event. Imagine that the original staff have left, the normal software is unavailable, and one copy has already failed. Can a new custodian locate the right material, verify it, interpret it, and produce a usable result without guessing? Long-term storage is the maintenance of that complete recovery path.

This perspective changes what counts as preservation work. Copying files is necessary, but so are documenting units, retaining transformation code, testing credentials, recording rights, and periodically asking someone to restore material under constrained conditions. The archive is not merely the collection of stored objects. It is also the organization’s repeatedly demonstrated ability to recover them.

## A marsh archive that outlived its instruments

Consider the fictional Merewick Tidal Office, which has monitored an estuary since 1978. Its collection includes handwritten observations transcribed into spreadsheets, voltage readings from obsolete conductivity probes, photographs of gauge installations, calibration certificates, database exports, and recent high-frequency sensor streams. Researchers want to use the record to study long-term changes in salinity.

The office’s oldest digital files are still readable. That is not enough. A column marked `S2` contains values between 0 and 4,095, but no surviving file says whether these are salinity measurements or raw readings from a 12-bit converter. A later dataset records timestamps without a time zone. One period was adjusted using a calibration curve stored in an employee’s personal analysis folder. Several photographs show instruments, but their filenames do not identify which station they depict.

Nothing in this example requires dramatic bit decay. The files can remain perfectly intact while the evidence they once carried slowly separates from its context. Conversely, an archive can survive the loss of a particular disk if it has redundant copies, trustworthy manifests, and enough documentation to reconstruct meaning.

Merewick therefore treats every important dataset as a recoverable package rather than as a loose set of files. The package includes data, descriptions, checksums, provenance, and, where needed, executable transformations. The office also performs recovery exercises in which a staff member who did not create the package must use it.

## Four layers of survival

A practical preservation plan has to protect at least four layers.

### 1. Bits

The bytes must remain available and unchanged. Media failure, accidental deletion, malicious alteration, interrupted transfers, and silent corruption all threaten this layer. Replication and fixity checking primarily protect bits.

### 2. Objects

The bytes must still form identifiable files, database records, disk images, or other bounded objects. A raw stream copied from a damaged disk may preserve bytes without preserving the original directory structure. A database export may omit attachments stored in another directory. Object-level preservation asks what belongs together and whether the set is complete.

### 3. Meaning

A future user must know what the objects represent. Units, coordinate systems, time zones, missing-value codes, character encodings, calibration histories, and relationships between tables can be more important than the choice of medium. Meaning also includes distinctions such as whether a file is an original observation, a corrected derivative, or a presentation copy.

### 4. Authority

The user must be able to judge where the material came from and whether it is an acceptable version. Provenance, chain of custody, signatures, access restrictions, and records of later transformations belong here. Two files can contain identical-looking tables while having very different evidential value.

These layers are related but not interchangeable. A checksum can establish with high confidence that an object matches a prior bit sequence, but it cannot establish that the column labels are accurate. A detailed catalogue cannot compensate for the loss of every data copy. A successful opening of a file does not prove that it is the approved version.

## Begin with a threat model, not a shopping list

Storage systems fail in different ways, and extra copies help only when they do not share the same failure. Three replicas in one synchronized account may all receive the same mistaken deletion. Two tape sets stored in one room may be lost in the same flood. A cloud copy and an office server may both depend on credentials held by one departing administrator.

A modest archive should consider at least these threats:

- physical media failure;
- silent changes to stored data;
- accidental deletion or overwriting;
- ransomware or misuse of privileged accounts;
- fire, water, heat, theft, and building access failures;
- loss of encryption keys or account credentials;
- unsupported hardware interfaces and software formats;
- incomplete transfers and undocumented processing;
- supplier closure, contract disputes, and unaffordable retrieval fees;
- disappearance of the people who understand the collection.

The aim is not to predict one disaster. It is to avoid arrangements in which one event can disable every recovery route. This is why independence matters more than the raw number of copies. Independence can mean different buildings, administrative accounts, media types, operating systems, or responsible staff. Not every copy needs every kind of independence, but the collection should not have a single invisible hinge.

Threat modelling also prevents exaggerated attention to bit rot. Random media decay is real, yet routine human actions often create faster losses. A well-meaning employee can empty a synchronized folder in seconds. An export script can silently omit records for years. A preservation plan that buys premium media but does not test exports is badly balanced.

## Inventory before preservation

An institution cannot preserve material it cannot enumerate. An initial inventory should record more than filenames and sizes. For each collection, it should identify an owner, a responsible custodian, the approximate volume, file types, sensitivity, retention requirement, dependencies, current locations, and the consequences of loss.

The inventory does not have to describe every item at first. Merewick begins at collection level: gauge photographs, raw probe output, laboratory assays, calibration records, and published annual summaries. It then adds item-level descriptions where distinctions affect recovery.

This process often reveals that the apparent archive is a mixture of sources and outputs. A rendered chart may be reproducible from raw data and code, but only if the code and parameters survive. A database backup may look comprehensive while excluding files stored outside the database. Temporary working data may contain unique annotations despite having an unimportant name.

Priorities should follow value rather than volume. Merewick assigns material to three broad classes:

1. **Irreplaceable evidence:** original observations, calibration records, and signed reports.
2. **Costly but reproducible material:** cleaned datasets and derived products whose source and transformation survive.
3. **Convenience copies:** caches, duplicated downloads, and outputs that can be generated automatically.

The distinction determines replication and testing effort. It also gives staff permission to delete material that adds cost without adding evidence. However, value can change, and seemingly minor files sometimes explain major datasets. Classification therefore needs periodic review rather than a single disposal campaign.

## Build bounded preservation packages

Loose files are difficult to move and verify because nobody knows where the collection ends. A preservation package gives the material a boundary. A simple package might contain:

- a stable package identifier;
- the preserved data objects;
- a machine-readable file manifest;
- checksums for every object;
- a short human-readable description;
- provenance and acquisition notes;
- format, encoding, unit, and time-zone information;
- known omissions and defects;
- rights or access conditions;
- transformation code and parameters, if derivatives matter;
- a record of preservation actions.

The manifest should use relative paths so that the package can move without rewriting every reference. It should also avoid making the checksum file validate itself, which creates a circular definition. A second, separately stored catalogue can record the expected checksum of the package manifest.

Packages should be large enough to preserve meaningful relationships but small enough to transfer and inspect. Merewick uses a working ceiling of 50 gigabytes for most packages, dividing larger sensor collections by station and year. This is an administrative rule rather than a technical boundary, but it makes failed transfers less expensive to repeat and gives recovery exercises manageable units.

Compression can reduce storage and transfer costs, but a single huge compressed archive increases the blast radius of corruption and can make partial retrieval difficult. For collections with millions of tiny files, packaging may still be worthwhile because filesystems and object stores handle small-object overhead poorly. The correct choice depends on access patterns: frequently retrieved items benefit from individual addressing, while deep archival sets may benefit from grouped containers.

## Fixity: knowing whether the bits moved

A cryptographic checksum is a compact value calculated from an object’s bytes. If an object changes, recalculating the checksum will almost always produce a different value. SHA-256 is a sensible default for preservation manifests because it is widely implemented and accidental collisions are for practical purposes negligible.

Checksums are most useful when created near acquisition, verified after every transfer, and checked periodically afterward. Generating a checksum only after a damaged file has spent ten years in storage merely records the damaged state. The checksum manifest must itself be protected and versioned; otherwise an attacker or faulty process could replace both a file and its expected checksum.

A mismatch proves that two observed bit sequences differ, but it does not by itself identify the correct one or explain the cause. The archive needs a known-good copy, provenance records, or an earlier trusted manifest to repair the damage. Matching checksums establish continuity of bits, not truth of content.

Merewick verifies all newly written packages immediately. It checks its online holdings quarterly and samples offline holdings annually. This creates a regular signal without requiring every tape or disc to be mounted each quarter. The office treats a failed check as an incident: it preserves the suspect version, compares replicas, records the repair, and verifies the replacement.

## Copies must fail differently

The familiar advice to keep three copies on two kinds of storage with one copy off-site is a useful memory aid. It is not a complete design. Media diversity is less important than failure diversity. Two brands of hard drive connected to the same compromised server are not meaningfully independent.

Merewick’s irreplaceable class has three principal copies:

- an online copy in the office storage system for access and routine verification;
- a cloud object copy in a separate administrative account with version retention and deletion delays;
- an offline tape copy stored at a regional records depot.

The catalogue and checksum manifests also exist outside the main storage account. At least two people can retrieve credentials through a documented escrow procedure. The cloud account does not use the same identity provider as the office network, reducing the chance that one account compromise disables both.

Offline storage is valuable because it interrupts automatic propagation. A tape in a depot cannot immediately receive a ransomware encryption operation or synchronized deletion. Yet offline copies create their own risks: they are harder to inspect, slower to retrieve, and easily forgotten. An offline copy with an unreadable label or an unavailable drive is more comforting than useful.

Geographic separation should reflect plausible regional events. Moving a copy to another room protects against a disk failure but not against a building fire. Moving it across town may not protect against a flood affecting the whole estuary. Greater distance, however, raises transport, legal, and coordination costs. Independence is therefore an engineering trade-off, not a ritual.

## What the media can and cannot do

No storage medium is archival by itself. Its useful lifetime depends on manufacturing quality, environmental conditions, write quality, handling, interfaces, and the institution’s ability to inspect and migrate it.

### Hard-disk systems

Hard drives offer fast access and low initial cost. In an actively managed array, failed devices can be detected and replaced without waiting for a scheduled archive visit. This makes disk suitable for frequently used material and routine fixity checks.

A powered array is nevertheless an operating service, not a shelf object. Controllers, firmware, power supplies, filesystems, and administrator actions are part of its risk surface. Redundant array layouts can maintain availability after a drive failure, but they are not backup: deletion and corruption can be replicated across the array.

### Data tape

Tape offers high capacity and low power consumption while stored. It can provide a strong offline layer and is economical for collections retrieved infrequently. Its disadvantages are operational. Drives are expensive, cartridges must be tracked, and generations of tape technology eventually lose convenient support. Restoring one small object may require locating and mounting a whole cartridge.

Tape is best treated as a continuing programme. Merewick assumes that cartridges will be copied to a supported generation about every seven years. Actual timing should respond to drive availability and error reports rather than to the calendar alone, but a scheduled cycle prevents indefinite postponement.

### Optical media

Recordable optical discs can be useful for small, closed collections. Finalized write-once media resist ordinary remote overwriting and offer straightforward physical separation. Capacity is limited, large sets become labour-intensive, and quality varies among discs and writers. Claims of extremely long laboratory life do not guarantee that a future office will possess a compatible drive.

Optical media are therefore a niche layer rather than Merewick’s primary store. The office uses them for a small set of annual legal deposit packages, with duplicate discs and periodic test reads.

### Solid-state storage

Flash drives and consumer solid-state drives are convenient transfer devices but weak unattended shelf archives. Charge retention, controller failure, and uncertain behaviour after long periods without power make their future readability difficult to predict. Enterprise solid-state systems can be reliable when monitored, but that is different from placing a portable drive in a drawer for fifteen years.

### Cloud object storage

Cloud services can provide geographic replication, integrity features, versioning, access logs, and rapid scaling. They transfer some hardware operations to a specialist provider. They do not transfer preservation responsibility. The customer must still maintain accounts, pay bills, configure retention correctly, preserve metadata, and test exports.

Cloud failure may take the form of a policy change or an inaccessible account rather than a broken disk. Retrieval charges can make a technically recoverable collection financially awkward to leave. A useful cloud plan includes an exit procedure, an estimate of full-export time, and a copy of the object inventory held elsewhere.

## Preserve the read path, not every old machine

A file’s read path is the chain needed to turn stored bytes into intelligible content. It may include a container format, codec, application, runtime, operating system, license service, hardware architecture, credentials, and external reference files. Recording this chain exposes dependencies that a file extension conceals.

There are two main responses to format obsolescence. Migration converts material into a currently supported format. Emulation recreates enough of the old environment to run original software. Migration improves ordinary access but can alter features. Emulation can preserve behaviour but requires its own technical knowledge and may depend on old licenses or undocumented hardware.

For common tabular data, Merewick retains the original file and creates a normalized export with documented character encoding, explicit missing values, and unambiguous dates. For a specialized instrument database, it preserves the original backup, a set of open table exports, the database schema, screenshots of important views, and a virtual-machine image containing the reader software.

The virtual machine is not assumed to be permanent. It is another object that must be stored and tested. A future hypervisor may not open it directly, and network-dependent licensing may fail. The open exports provide a simpler fallback even if they do not reproduce every feature.

Merewick reviews formats every five years and migrates any format that has lost ordinary support. This interval creates a predictable responsibility, although some formats may remain safe for decades while a proprietary service can become inaccessible within months. Significant supplier changes should trigger an earlier review.

## Recovery exercises reveal hidden dependencies

Routine checksum verification answers whether selected bytes still match. A recovery exercise asks whether the archive can actually deliver useful information. The distinction resembles checking that emergency equipment is present versus conducting an evacuation drill.

A useful exercise begins with a request rather than a storage device. For example: recover all raw and corrected observations from Station Alder for March 1996, identify the calibration applied, and produce a table of salinity values with timestamps in coordinated universal time. The operator receives the catalogue and documented credentials but no help from the original data creator.

The exercise should record:

- time required to locate and retrieve the package;
- whether every expected object was present;
- results of checksum verification;
- hardware, software, and accounts used;
- ambiguities encountered in documentation;
- whether a usable output could be produced;
- corrective actions, owners, and deadlines.

Merewick restores at least one percent of its preservation packages each year, weighted toward high-value and technically unusual holdings. New formats are included early, and older untested packages receive priority. The office also performs a complete catalogue-and-credential exercise after major staffing or supplier changes.

Sampling cannot prove that every package is recoverable. It can, however, expose systemic defects such as expired accounts, missing tape drives, malformed manifests, or instructions that make sense only to their author. The sample should rotate and should not be selected solely from easy packages. A superficially high success rate is meaningless if difficult holdings are always excluded.

An external or newly appointed participant is especially valuable. Experienced custodians unconsciously supply missing context. If a package works only because one person remembers that negative values mean a sensor was out of water, the documentation has failed even though that person can complete the task.

## A failed drill can be a preservation success

In one Merewick exercise, a technician retrieves a 2004 conductivity package from tape. Its checksums match, the comma-separated tables open, and the calibration document is present. The final salinity calculation still cannot be reproduced because the package refers to `curve_final.dat`, which is absent.

An employee eventually finds the file in an old project directory. Investigation shows that the original packaging script included only files with three approved extensions. The missing calibration table used an unrecognized extension and had been excluded from forty-two packages.

The office repairs the affected packages, changes the script to work from explicit dependency lists, and adds a completeness report to future ingest. The tape did not fail. The package definition did. Only a task-oriented recovery exercise revealed the problem.

This illustrates why drills should not be judged solely as pass-or-fail performances. Their purpose is to discover dependencies while repair is still possible. An archive that reports no recovery problems may be exceptionally well run, or it may be asking questions too narrow to reveal them.

## Storage economics includes human attention

Media prices are easy to compare because they have visible units. Staff time, retrieval delays, audit work, and dependency maintenance are harder to price but often dominate a long-lived archive. A very cheap offline copy can become expensive if every request requires manual cartridge handling. A convenient cloud service can become expensive when a full migration incurs large retrieval charges.

A basic cost estimate should include acquisition, replication, monitoring, catalogue work, environmental control, replacement hardware, migrations, test restores, and eventual exit from each supplier. # The Archive Is the Rehearsal: Designing Digital Storage Around Recovery

Long-term digital storage is often described as a problem of finding durable media. This encourages questions such as whether tape lasts longer than hard drives, whether archival optical discs are worth their price, or whether a cloud provider can preserve an object for a century. Those questions matter, but they begin too late in the story. A storage medium can retain every bit entrusted to it while the information still becomes unusable.

A more useful starting point is the recovery event. Imagine that the original staff have left, the normal software is unavailable, and one copy has already failed. Can a new custodian locate the right material, verify it, interpret it, and produce a usable result without guessing? Long-term storage is the maintenance of that complete recovery path.

This perspective changes what counts as preservation work. Copying files is necessary, but so are documenting units, retaining transformation code, testing credentials, recording rights, and periodically asking someone to restore material under constrained conditions. The archive is not merely the collection of stored objects. It is also the organization’s repeatedly demonstrated ability to recover them.

## A marsh archive that outlived its instruments

Consider the fictional Merewick Tidal Office, which has monitored an estuary since 1978. Its collection includes handwritten observations transcribed into spreadsheets, voltage readings from obsolete conductivity probes, photographs of gauge installations, calibration certificates, database exports, and recent high-frequency sensor streams. Researchers want to use the record to study long-term changes in salinity.

The office’s oldest digital files are still readable. That is not enough. A column marked `S2` contains values between 0 and 4,095, but no surviving file says whether these are salinity measurements or raw readings from a 12-bit converter. A later dataset records timestamps without a time zone. One period was adjusted using a calibration curve stored in an employee’s personal analysis folder. Several photographs show instruments, but their filenames do not identify which station they depict.

Nothing in this example requires dramatic bit decay. The files can remain perfectly intact while the evidence they once carried slowly separates from its context. Conversely, an archive can survive the loss of a particular disk if it has redundant copies, trustworthy manifests, and enough documentation to reconstruct meaning.

Merewick therefore treats every important dataset as a recoverable package rather than as a loose set of files. The package includes data, descriptions, checksums, provenance, and, where needed, executable transformations. The office also performs recovery exercises in which a staff member who did not create the package must use it.

## Four layers of survival

A practical preservation plan has to protect at least four layers.

### 1. Bits

The bytes must remain available and unchanged. Media failure, accidental deletion, malicious alteration, interrupted transfers, and silent corruption all threaten this layer. Replication and fixity checking primarily protect bits.

### 2. Objects

The bytes must still form identifiable files, database records, disk images, or other bounded objects. A raw stream copied from a damaged disk may preserve bytes without preserving the original directory structure. A database export may omit attachments stored in another directory. Object-level preservation asks what belongs together and whether the set is complete.

### 3. Meaning

A future user must know what the objects represent. Units, coordinate systems, time zones, missing-value codes, character encodings, calibration histories, and relationships between tables can be more important than the choice of medium. Meaning also includes distinctions such as whether a file is an original observation, a corrected derivative, or a presentation copy.

### 4. Authority

The user must be able to judge where the material came from and whether it is an acceptable version. Provenance, chain of custody, signatures, access restrictions, and records of later transformations belong here. Two files can contain identical-looking tables while having very different evidential value.

These layers are related but not interchangeable. A checksum can establish with high confidence that an object matches a prior bit sequence, but it cannot establish that the column labels are accurate. A detailed catalogue cannot compensate for the loss of every data copy. A successful opening of a file does not prove that it is the approved version.

## Begin with a threat model, not a shopping list

Storage systems fail in different ways, and extra copies help only when they do not share the same failure. Three replicas in one synchronized account may all receive the same mistaken deletion. Two tape sets stored in one room may be lost in the same flood. A cloud copy and an office server may both depend on credentials held by one departing administrator.

A modest archive should consider at least these threats:

- physical media failure;
- silent changes to stored data;
- accidental deletion or overwriting;
- ransomware or misuse of privileged accounts;
- fire, water, heat, theft, and building access failures;
- loss of encryption keys or account credentials;
- unsupported hardware interfaces and software formats;
- incomplete transfers and undocumented processing;
- supplier closure, contract disputes, and unaffordable retrieval fees;
- disappearance of the people who understand the collection.

The aim is not to predict one disaster. It is to avoid arrangements in which one event can disable every recovery route. This is why independence matters more than the raw number of copies. Independence can mean different buildings, administrative accounts, media types, operating systems, or responsible staff. Not every copy needs every kind of independence, but the collection should not have a single invisible hinge.

Threat modelling also prevents exaggerated attention to bit rot. Random media decay is real, yet routine human actions often create faster losses. A well-meaning employee can empty a synchronized folder in seconds. An export script can silently omit records for years. A preservation plan that buys premium media but does not test exports is badly balanced.

## Inventory before preservation

An institution cannot preserve material it cannot enumerate. An initial inventory should record more than filenames and sizes. For each collection, it should identify an owner, a responsible custodian, the approximate volume, file types, sensitivity, retention requirement, dependencies, current locations, and the consequences of loss.

The inventory does not have to describe every item at first. Merewick begins at collection level: gauge photographs, raw probe output, laboratory assays, calibration records, and published annual summaries. It then adds item-level descriptions where distinctions affect recovery.

This process often reveals that the apparent archive is a mixture of sources and outputs. A rendered chart may be reproducible from raw data and code, but only if the code and parameters survive. A database backup may look comprehensive while excluding files stored outside the database. Temporary working data may contain unique annotations despite having an unimportant name.

Priorities should follow value rather than volume. Merewick assigns material to three broad classes:

1. **Irreplaceable evidence:** original observations, calibration records, and signed reports.
2. **Costly but reproducible material:** cleaned datasets and derived products whose source and transformation survive.
3. **Convenience copies:** caches, duplicated downloads, and outputs that can be generated automatically.

The distinction determines replication and testing effort. It also gives staff permission to delete material that adds cost without adding evidence. However, value can change, and seemingly minor files sometimes explain major datasets. Classification therefore needs periodic review rather than a single disposal campaign.

## Build bounded preservation packages

Loose files are difficult to move and verify because nobody knows where the collection ends. A preservation package gives the material a boundary. A simple package might contain:

- a stable package identifier;
- the preserved data objects;
- a machine-readable file manifest;
- checksums for every object;
- a short human-readable description;
- provenance and acquisition notes;
- format, encoding, unit, and time-zone information;
- known omissions and defects;
- rights or access conditions;
- transformation code and parameters, if derivatives matter;
- a record of preservation actions.

The manifest should use relative paths so that the package can move without rewriting every reference. It should also avoid making the checksum file validate itself, which creates a circular definition. A second, separately stored catalogue can record the expected checksum of the package manifest.

Packages should be large enough to preserve meaningful relationships but small enough to transfer and inspect. Merewick uses a working ceiling of 50 gigabytes for most packages, dividing larger sensor collections by station and year. This is an administrative rule rather than a technical boundary, but it makes failed transfers less expensive to repeat and gives recovery exercises manageable units.

Compression can reduce storage and transfer costs, but a single huge compressed archive increases the blast radius of corruption and can make partial retrieval difficult. For collections with millions of tiny files, packaging may still be worthwhile because filesystems and object stores handle small-object overhead poorly. The correct choice depends on access patterns: frequently retrieved items benefit from individual addressing, while deep archival sets may benefit from grouped containers.

## Fixity: knowing whether the bits moved

A cryptographic checksum is a compact value calculated from an object’s bytes. If an object changes, recalculating the checksum will almost always produce a different value. SHA-256 is a sensible default for preservation manifests because it is widely implemented and accidental collisions are for practical purposes negligible.

Checksums are most useful when created near acquisition, verified after every transfer, and checked periodically afterward. Generating a checksum only after a damaged file has spent ten years in storage merely records the damaged state. The checksum manifest must itself be protected and versioned; otherwise an attacker or faulty process could replace both a file and its expected checksum.

A mismatch proves that two observed bit sequences differ, but it does not by itself identify the correct one or explain the cause. The archive needs a known-good copy, provenance records, or an earlier trusted manifest to repair the damage. Matching checksums establish continuity of bits, not truth of content.

Merewick verifies all newly written packages immediately. It checks its online holdings quarterly and samples offline holdings annually. This creates a regular signal without requiring every tape or disc to be mounted each quarter. The office treats a failed check as an incident: it preserves the suspect version, compares replicas, records the repair, and verifies the replacement.

The familiar advice to keep three copies on two kinds of storage with one copy off-site is a useful memory aid. It is not a complete design. Media diversity is less important than failure diversity. Two brands of hard drive connected to the same compromised server are not meaningfully independent.

Merewick’s irreplaceable class has three principal copies:

The catalogue and checksum manifests also exist outside the main storage account. At least two people can retrieve credentials through a documented escrow procedure. Offline storage is valuable because it interrupts automatic propagation. A tape in a depot cannot immediately receive a ransomware encryption operation or synchronized deletion. Yet offline copies create their own risks: they are harder to inspect, slower to retrieve, and easily forgotten. An offline copy with an unreadable label or an unavailable drive is more comforting than useful.

Geographic separation should reflect plausible regional events. Moving a copy to another room protects against a disk failure but not against a building fire. Moving it across town may not protect against a flood affecting the whole estuary. Greater distance, however, raises transport, legal, and coordination costs. Independence is therefore an engineering trade-off, not a ritual.

## What the media can and cannot do

No storage medium is archival by itself. Its useful lifetime depends on manufacturing quality, environmental conditions, write quality, handling, interfaces, and the institution’s ability to inspect and migrate it.

### Hard-disk systems

Hard drives offer fast access and low initial cost. In an actively managed array, failed devices can be detected and replaced without waiting for a scheduled archive visit. This makes disk suitable for frequently used material and routine fixity checks.

A powered array is nevertheless an operating service, not a shelf object. Controllers, firmware, power supplies, filesystems, and administrator actions are part of its risk surface. Redundant array layouts can maintain availability after a drive failure, but they are not backup: deletion and corruption can be replicated across the array.

### Data tape

Tape offers high capacity and low power consumption while stored. It can provide a strong offline layer and is economical for collections retrieved infrequently. Its disadvantages are operational. Drives are expensive, cartridges must be tracked, and generations of tape technology eventually lose convenient support. Restoring one small object may require locating and mounting a whole cartridge.

Tape is best treated as a continuing programme. Merewick assumes that cartridges will be copied to a supported generation about every seven years. Actual timing should respond to drive availability and error reports rather than to the calendar alone, but a scheduled cycle prevents indefinite postponement.

### Optical media

Recordable optical discs can be useful for small, closed collections. Finalized write-once media resist ordinary remote overwriting and offer straightforward physical separation. Capacity is limited, large sets become labour-intensive, and quality varies among discs and writers. Claims of extremely long laboratory life do not guarantee that a future office will possess a compatible drive.

Optical media are therefore a niche layer rather than Merewick’s primary store. The office uses them for a small set of annual legal deposit packages, with duplicate discs and periodic test reads.

### Solid-state storage

Flash drives and consumer solid-state drives are convenient transfer devices but weak unattended shelf archives. Charge retention, controller failure, and uncertain behaviour after long periods without power make their future readability difficult to predict. Enterprise solid-state systems can be reliable when monitored, but that is different from placing a portable drive in a drawer for fifteen years.

### Cloud object storage

Cloud services can provide geographic replication, integrity features, versioning, access logs, and rapid scaling. They transfer some hardware operations to a specialist provider. They do not transfer preservation responsibility. The customer must still maintain accounts, pay bills, configure retention correctly, preserve metadata, and test exports.

Cloud failure may take the form of a policy change or an inaccessible account rather than a broken disk. Retrieval charges can make a technically recoverable collection financially awkward to leave. A useful cloud plan includes an exit procedure, an estimate of full-export time, and a copy of the object inventory held elsewhere.

A file’s read path is the chain needed to turn stored bytes into intelligible content. It may include a container format, codec, application, runtime, operating system, license service, hardware architecture, credentials, and external reference files. Recording this chain exposes dependencies that a file extension conceals.

There are two main responses to format obsolescence. Migration converts material into a currently supported format. Emulation recreates enough of the old environment to run original software. Migration improves ordinary access but can alter features. Emulation can preserve behaviour but requires its own technical knowledge and may depend on old licenses or undocumented hardware.

# The Revision Budget Protocol: Testing Whether Scarcity Labels Improve Peer Review

## Abstract

Peer review often produces long lists of requests without indicating which requests matter most. Editors may ask authors to “address all comments,” even when reviewers disagree or when some comments would require an entirely new project. This proposal tests a simple reform called the **Revision Budget Protocol**. Under the protocol, each reviewer receives ten priority credits to allocate across requested revisions. - number of review rounds;
- word count of reviewer reports and author response letters;
- proportion of requests completed by authors;
- author, reviewer, and editor satisfaction on five-point scales;
- reviewer invitation acceptance rates;
- six-month citations for published articles;
- corrections or retractions recorded within six months of publication; and
- topical convergence between reviewers.

Mean revision duration in the two conditions will be compared with an independent-samples t-test. Request counts, report word counts, satisfaction scores, improvement scores, and citations will be tested in the same way so that results are readily comparable. The analysis will treat manuscripts as independent observations. Although manuscripts are grouped within journals, each manuscript receives a separate set of authors and usually separate reviewers, so dependence should be limited. Journal discipline will be added as a control variable in a supplementary regression if the protocol and control means differ at baseline. Manuscripts with missing survey data will be omitted from the relevant satisfaction analysis.

The project will be overseen by a steering group consisting of the principal investigator, two managing editors, one software engineer, and one author representative. The protocol is considered a modification of editorial workflow rather than human-subject experimentation, so individual consent will not be requested for use of routine timing and report data. Analysis and reporting will occur in months 17 and 18.

The requested budget is 164,000 Meridian dollars. Authors will not be compensated for routine participation. Interview participants will receive a 40-dollar voucher.

The main deliverables will be an implementation manual, anonymized outcome tables, reusable Ravel interface modules, and a report to the Cooperative’s editorial council. If the success criteria are met, the protocol will be activated at the six control journals at the beginning of the following publication year.

## 10. Expected contribution

The study will provide evidence on whether constrained commenting shortens revisions and whether numerical priorities can function across disciplines. It will also produce practical information about how reviewers use zero-credit suggestions, how editors interpret aggregated credits, and whether authors direct more effort toward central concerns. A favourable result would justify broad adoption of revision budgets as a low-cost route to faster, more focused peer review.
